By (c), F_ε and F are H^k⌞M-integrable, so by countable additivity (g_ε)_#X(ω) = Σ_ia_i(ε) and S(ω) = ∫_MF dH^k = Σ_ia_i, where a_i(ε) := ∫_{G_i}F_ε dH^k, a_i := ∫_{G_i}F dH^k; and |a_i(ε)|, |a_i| ≤ b_i := ∫_{G_i}G dH^k with Σ_ib_i = ∫_MG dH^k < ∞, for all 0 < ε ≤ ε₀.
 (f) (Convergence on one piece: weak continuity of minors.) Fix i; write Φ = Φ_i, Ω = Ω_i, N = N_{j(i)}, u_ε := g_ε∘Φ (C¹ on Ω, ‖Du_ε‖ ≤ 2Λ) and u := g∘Φ (Lipschitz on Ω; by Rademacher's theorem and the definition of d^Mg via C¹ charts, u is differentiable at Lᵏ-a.e. w ∈ Φ⁻¹(G_i) with Du(w) = d^Mg_{Φ(w)}∘DΦ(w) — only such w are used). Then |u_ε − u| ≤ Λε on Ω. For H^k-a.e. x = Φ(w) ∈ G_i, ξ(x) is a unit simple k-vector orienting T_xM = T_xN = DΦ(w)(ℝ^k) (orientation property of the triple, Ch. 3, Remark 1.5(2) and Remark 1.8(1) together with the Upper Density Theorem Ch. 1, 3.6, which identify the weighted tangent space of (M,θ) with T_xN at H^k-a.e. x ∈ M_j), so ξ(Φ(w)) = c(w)·∂₁Φ(w)∧⋯∧∂_kΦ(w) with c(w) := ⟨ξ(Φ(w)), ∂₁Φ∧⋯∧∂_kΦ⟩/|∂₁Φ∧⋯∧∂_kΦ|² measurable and |c(w)| = 1/JΦ(w) (|∂₁Φ∧⋯∧∂_kΦ| = JΦ). By the chain rule Dg_ε(Φ(w))∂_bΦ(w) = ∂_bu_ε(w), hence Dg_ε(x)_#ξ(x) = c(w)·∂₁u_ε(w)∧⋯∧∂_ku_ε(w), whose coordinates are the k×k minors M_γ(Du_ε(w)) (γ ∈ I(k,D′)); likewise L(x)_#ξ(x) = c(w)·∂₁u(w)∧⋯∧∂_ku(w) at a.e. w. By the area formula for the injective C¹ map Φ (change of variables, Simon Ch. 2, 3.4) and (a)–(b) (which allow inserting 1_{K″}), for 0 < ε ≤ ε₀:
 a_i(ε) = Σ_γ∫_Ωψ(w)·ω_γ(u_ε(w))·M_γ(Du_ε(w)) dw,  a_i = Σ_γ∫_Ωψ(w)·ω_γ(u(w))·M_γ(Du(w)) dw,
 where ω_γ := ω(e_γ) and ψ(w) := 1_{Φ⁻¹(G_i∩K″)}(w)·θ(Φ(w))·c(w)·JΦ(w). Here |ψ| = θ∘Φ·1_{Φ⁻¹(G_i∩K″)}, so ∫_Ω|ψ|dw ≤ ∫_{Φ⁻¹(G_i∩K″)}θ(Φ(w))JΦ(w)dw = ∫_{G_i∩K″}θ dH^k < ∞ (JΦ ≥ 1): ψ ∈ L¹(Ω).
 Weak continuity of minors. Claim: if v_ε, v : Ω → ℝ^{D′} are Lipschitz, sup_ε‖Dv_ε‖_∞ < ∞ and v_ε → v uniformly, then every r×r minor M(Dv_ε) (rows a₁,…,a_r, columns b₁,…,b_r) converges to M(Dv) weakly-* in L^∞(Ω), i.e. ∫ηM(Dv_ε) → ∫ηM(Dv) for every η ∈ L¹(Ω). Proof by induction on r. Since the minors are bounded in L^∞ uniformly in ε and C_c^∞(Ω) is dense in L¹(Ω), it suffices to take η = φ ∈ C_c^∞(Ω). r = 1: ∫φ∂_bv_ε^a = −∫v_ε^a∂_bφ → −∫v^a∂_bφ = ∫φ∂_bv^a. r ≥ 2: let C_q (q = 1,…,r) be the cofactors of the first row, i.e. ± the (r−1)×(r−1) minors with rows a₂,…,a_r and columns {b₁,…,b_r}∖{b_q}. For smooth maps the Piola identity Σ_q∂_{b_q}C_q = 0 holds (the second derivatives cancel in pairs by symmetry), so M(Dv) = Σ_q∂_{b_q}v^{a₁}C_q = Σ_q∂_{b_q}(v^{a₁}C_q); for Lipschitz maps this identity holds in the sense of distributions (mollify v: v^δ → v locally uniformly, Dv^δ → Dv a.e. and boundedly, so all products converge in L¹_loc). Hence ∫φM(Dv_ε) = −Σ_q∫v_ε^{a₁}C_q(Dv_ε)∂_{b_q}φ. Now ∫v_ε^{a₁}C_q(Dv_ε)∂_{b_q}φ − ∫v^{a₁}C_q(Dv)∂_{b_q}φ = ∫(v_ε^{a₁} − v^{a₁})C_q(Dv_ε)∂_{b_q}φ + ∫v^{a₁}(C_q(Dv_ε) − C_q(Dv))∂_{b_q}φ → 0 (the first term by uniform convergence and the L^∞ bound, the second by the induction hypothesis tested against v^{a₁}∂_{b_q}φ ∈ L¹). So ∫φM(Dv_ε) → −Σ_q∫v^{a₁}C_q(Dv)∂_{b_q}φ = ∫φM(Dv).
 Apply this with v_ε := u_ε, v := u, r = k. Then ∫ψ(ω_γ∘u_ε)M_γ(Du_ε) − ∫ψ(ω_γ∘u)M_γ(Du) = ∫ψ(ω_γ∘u_ε − ω_γ∘u)M_γ(Du_ε) + ∫ψ(ω_γ∘u)(M_γ(Du_ε) − M_γ(Du)) → 0: the first term is ≤ ‖ψ‖_{L¹}·sup_Ω|ω_γ∘u_ε − ω_γ∘u|·k!(2Λ)^k → 0 (ω_γ is uniformly continuous and |u_ε − u| ≤ Λε), the second → 0 by weak-* convergence tested against ψ·(ω_γ∘u) ∈ L¹(Ω). Hence a_i(ε) → a_i as ε ↓ 0.
 (g) (Summation over the pieces.) By (e), (f) and dominated convergence for series (Tannery's theorem: |a_i(ε)| ≤ b_i, Σ_ib_i < ∞, a_i(ε) → a_i), along every sequence ε_m ↓ 0, (g_ε)_#X(ω) = Σ_ia_i(ε) → Σ_ia_i = S(ω). Since g_#X(ω) = lim_{ε↓0}(g_ε)_#X(ω) by definition (A2(e)), g_#X(ω) = S(ω) for every ω, i.e. g_#X = S. (For k = 0, A2(e) defines g_#X(φ) := X(φ∘g) directly; then (I) is immediate from the representation of the signed measure X as θξH^0⌞M, since L(x)_# is the identity on 0-vectors.)
Proof of (II): g_#X is integer multiplicity.
 (II.1) (The sibling push-forward.) Apply `LipschitzPushforwardIntegerMultiplicity`, its ambient dimensions and degree instantiated as D, D′ and k, with U := ℝ^D, V := ℝ^{D′} (both open), T := X and f := g. Its hypotheses hold: X is integer multiplicity; g is Lipschitz, hence locally Lipschitz on U; g maps U into V; and for every compact K ⊆ V the set g⁻¹(K) ∩ spt X is compact (properness of g|spt X). It yields an integer multiplicity current S̃ ∈ D_k(ℝ^{D′}) with `IsLipschitzPushforward X g S̃`, i.e. there are M′, θ′, ξ′, L′ such that
  (II.1a) `IsRectifiableTriple univ k M′ θ′ ξ′` (U = ℝ^D): M′ is H^k-measurable and countably k-rectifiable, θ′(x) > 0 for x ∈ M′, θ′ is H^k-integrable on M′ ∩ K for every compact K, ξ′ is H^k⌞M′-measurable, and for H^k-a.e. x ∈ M′, ξ′(x) = ±simpleNVector τ′ for an orthonormal k-frame τ′ spanning a weighted approximate tangent space of (M′,θ′) at x. Nothing more is known about θ′: it is real valued, and it need not be integer valued or ≥ 1;
  (II.1b) X(ω) = ∫_{M′}θ′⟨ω, ξ′⟩dH^k for every ω ∈ D^k(ℝ^D);
  (II.1c) for H^k-a.e. x ∈ M′, every subspace Π with `HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt k M′ θ′ x Π` and every v ∈ Π, the map t ↦ g(x + tv) has derivative L′(x)v at t = 0;
  (II.1d) S̃(ω) = ∫_{M′}θ′⟨ω(g(x)), L′(x)_#ξ′(x)⟩dH^k for every ω ∈ D^k(ℝ^{D′}).
 By (I) it suffices to prove S̃ = S: then g_#X and S̃ take the same value on every test form, and `IsIntegerMultiplicity` only refers to these values, so g_#X is integer multiplicity. Steps (II.2)–(II.7) compare the two representations (M,θ,ξ) (from `IsIntegerMultiplicity X`) and (M′,θ′,ξ′) (from (II.1a)–(II.1b)) of X; of θ′ only its positivity on M′ and its integrability on compact sets are used.
 (II.2) (Unit orienting k-vectors.) By the unit fact of the Conventions, |ξ| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M and |ξ′| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M′.
 (II.3) (The two vector measures agree on bounded Borel sets.) For γ ∈ I(k,D) and bounded Borel B ⊆ ℝ^D put Ξ^γ(B) := ∫_{B∩M}θξ^γ dH^k and Ξ′^γ(B) := ∫_{B∩M′}θ′ξ′^γ dH^k. These integrals converge absolutely (|ξ^γ| ≤ |ξ| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M and θ is integrable on M ∩ B̄; likewise for θ′, ξ′ by (II.1a)), and for each R > 0, Ξ^γ and Ξ′^γ are finite signed (countably additive) measures on the Borel subsets of the open ball B_R(0). (1) For φ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^D) the form φdx^γ is a test form and ⟨φ(x)dx^γ, ξ(x)⟩ = φ(x)ξ^γ(x), so by the two representations of X (`IsIntegerMultiplicity X` and (II.1b)), ∫φ dΞ^γ = X(φdx^γ) = ∫φ dΞ′^γ. (2) For φ ∈ C_c(ℝ^D) the mollifications φ_ε := ϕ_ε * φ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^D) (0 < ε ≤ 1) converge uniformly to φ, satisfy |φ_ε| ≤ sup|φ| and are supported in the fixed compact set K := {dist(·, spt φ) ≤ 1}; dominated convergence (dominators sup|φ|·θ1_{M∩K} and sup|φ|·θ′1_{M′∩K}) gives ∫φ dΞ^γ = ∫φ dΞ′^γ. (3) For a compact set K_c ⊆ B_R(0) the functions φ_i(x) := max{0, 1 − i·dist(x, K_c)} are continuous with compact supports {dist(·, K_c) ≤ 1/i}, which lie in a fixed compact subset of B_R(0) for i ≥ i₀; 0 ≤ φ_i ≤ 1 and φ_i decreases pointwise to 1_{K_c}, so dominated convergence gives Ξ^γ(K_c) = Ξ′^γ(K_c). (4) The compact subsets of B_R(0) form a π-system generating the Borel σ-algebra of B_R(0) (every open subset of B_R(0) is a countable union of compact sets), and the Borel sets B ⊆ B_R(0) with Ξ^γ(B) = Ξ′^γ(B) form a Dynkin system: it contains B_R(0) (an increasing union of compact sets, by countable additivity) and is closed under relative complements and countable disjoint unions, Ξ^γ and Ξ′^γ being finite signed measures on B_R(0). By Dynkin's π-system theorem, Ξ^γ(B) = Ξ′^γ(B) for every Borel B ⊆ B_R(0), every R > 0 and every γ ∈ I(k,D).
 (II.4) (σ-finiteness of λ := H^k⌞(M ∪ M′), using only θ′ > 0 and the local integrability of θ′.) Let K_j := B̄_j(0) (j = 1, 2, …), compact with ⋃_jK_j = ℝ^D. Since θ is integrable on M ∩ K_j and θ′ is integrable on M′ ∩ K_j (II.1a), θ and θ′ are H^k-measurable on M ∩ K_j and M′ ∩ K_j respectively, and M, M′ are H^k-measurable; so for j, r ≥ 1 the sets
  A_{j,r} := M ∩ K_j ∩ {θ ≥ 1/r},  A′_{j,r} := M′ ∩ K_j ∩ {θ′ ≥ 1/r}
 are H^k-measurable, and by Chebyshev's (Markov's) inequality
  H^k(A′_{j,r}) ≤ r∫_{A′_{j,r}}θ′ dH^k ≤ r∫_{M′∩K_j}θ′ dH^k < ∞,  H^k(A_{j,r}) ≤ r∫_{M∩K_j}θ dH^k < ∞.
 Every x ∈ M ∪ M′ belongs to some A_{j,r} or A′_{j,r}: choose j ≥ |x|, and r ≥ 1/θ(x) if x ∈ M (θ(x) > 0), resp. r ≥ 1/θ′(x) if x ∈ M′ (θ′(x) > 0). Hence M ∪ M′ = ⋃_{j,r}(A_{j,r} ∪ A′_{j,r}) is a countable union of H^k-measurable sets of finite H^k-measure, and λ(ℝ^D ∖ (M ∪ M′)) = 0: λ is σ-finite. (No lower bound θ′ ≥ 1 is used; for the integer valued θ the sets A_{j,1} = M ∩ K_j alone would do.)
 (II.5) (Radon–Nikodym uniqueness.) The vector measures Ξ = (Ξ^γ)_γ and Ξ′ = (Ξ′^γ)_γ of (II.3) are absolutely continuous with respect to λ, with densities κ := θξ1_M and κ′ := θ′ξ′1_{M′}: Ξ^γ(B) = ∫_Bκ^γ dλ and Ξ′^γ(B) = ∫_Bκ′^γ dλ for bounded Borel B. The densities are λ-measurable (by the measurability of θ, θ′ in (II.4) and of ξ, ξ′ in the triple conditions) and λ-integrable on bounded sets (|κ| ≤ θ1_M and |κ′| ≤ θ′1_{M′} λ-a.e.). Since λ is σ-finite by (II.4) and H^k is Borel regular (Simon Ch. 1, 2.6), every λ-measurable set is the union of a Borel set and a λ-null set (Simon Ch. 1, 1.12 and 1.15(2), applied to the finite Borel regular measures H^k⌞A_{j,r} and H^k⌞A′_{j,r}, together with λ(ℝ^D ∖ (M ∪ M′)) = 0); hence κ^γ and κ′^γ agree λ-a.e. with Borel functions, and we may assume them Borel. For each j, the bounded Borel sets E_j^± := B_j(0) ∩ {±(κ^γ − κ′^γ) > 0} satisfy, by (II.3), ∫_{E_j^±}±(κ^γ − κ′^γ)dλ = ±(Ξ^γ(E_j^±) − Ξ′^γ(E_j^±)) = 0 with an integrand that is strictly positive on E_j^±, so λ(E_j^±) = 0. As {κ^γ ≠ κ′^γ} = ⋃_j(E_j^+ ∪ E_j^−), κ^γ = κ′^γ λ-a.e. for each of the finitely many γ ∈ I(k,D). By (17)–(19) (mass is continuous under M-convergence): (24) M(Q) ≤ cM(T), M(R₁) ≤ cM(T), M(S₁) ≤ cM(∂T); and since ∂ψ_#X_ν = ψ_#∂X_ν ⇀ ∂Q, lower semicontinuity of mass (2.14) gives (25) M(∂Q) ≤ liminf M(ψ_#∂X_ν) ≤ liminf[M(ψ_#(∂T − (∂T)_{σ_ν})) + M(ψ_#S_{σ_ν})] ≤ cM(∂T).
C7 (constancy on faces; (26)–(33)). Let F ∈ 𝓛_n with relative interior F̊, contained (after relabelling coordinates and translating) in ℝⁿ×{0}, and p the orthogonal projection onto ℝⁿ×{0}. Each y ∈ F̊ has a ball B_y with B_y ∩ L_n = B_y ∩ F̊ (dist(y, L_n ∖ F̊) > 0). On the open set ψ⁻¹(B_y) the map ψ takes values in B_y ∩ F̊ ⊆ ℝⁿ×{0} (after the translation), so its normal coordinates ψ^i (i > n) are constant there; hence for small ε the normal coordinates of the mollified maps ψ_ε used in A2(e) are constant on the compact part of spt X_ν mapped near spt ω, and for ω supported in B_y, ψ_ε^#ω only involves the dx¹∧⋯∧dxⁿ-coefficient of ω. Passing to the limits, Q⌞B_y = Q⌞(B_y ∩ F̊) and Q(ω) = Q(ω(e₁,…,e_n)·dx¹∧⋯∧dxⁿ) for ω supported in B_y, i.e. (26) Q⌞F̊ = p_#(Q⌞F̊) is an n-current carried by the plane of F with orienting n-vector ±e₁∧⋯∧e_n. Thus Q⌞F̊ is an n-current in the n-plane with ∂(Q⌞F̊) = ∂Q on each B_y, of finite mass in F̊. By A5(a) (the arguments of 2.34–2.35), (27) Q⌞F̊(ω) = ∫_{F̊}θ_F⟨ω, e₁∧⋯∧e_n⟩dLⁿ with θ_F ∈ BV(F̊), (28) M(Q⌞F̊) = ∫_{F̊}|θ_F|, M((∂Q)⌞F̊) = |Dθ_F|(F̊); θ_F is integer valued if Q is integer multiplicity. (29)–(30): Q⌞F̊ − β[[F]] has density θ_F − β on F̊, so M(Q⌞F̊ − β[[F]]) = ∫_{F̊}|θ_F − β| and M(∂(Q⌞F̊ − β[[F]])) = |D((θ_F − β)1_{F̊})|(ℝⁿ). (31) Choose β_F with min{Lⁿ{x ∈ F̊ : θ_F(x) ≥ β_F}, Lⁿ{x ∈ F̊ : θ_F(x) ≤ β_F}} ≥ ½ (Lⁿ(F̊) = 1), β_F ∈ ℤ if θ_F is integer valued, β_F = 0 if θ_F = 0 a.e. (32) By A6: M(Q⌞F̊ − β_F[[F]]) ≤ cM((∂Q)⌞F̊), M(∂(Q⌞F̊ − β_F[[F]])) ≤ cM((∂Q)⌞F̊). (33) By A5(b) (Hⁿ(L_{n−1}) = 0, M(Q) + M(∂Q) < ∞), Q⌞L_{n−1} = 0, so by (22) Q = Σ_{F∈𝓛_n}Q⌞F̊ (M-convergent, disjoint pieces).
C8 (the polyhedral chain; (34)–(38)). Let P := Σ_{F∈𝓛_n}β_F[[F]]. Summing (32) over F: (34) M(Q − P) ≤ cM(∂Q), M(∂Q − ∂P) ≤ cM(∂Q). By (31), |β_F| ≤ 2∫_{F̊}|θ_F| (35), so (36) M(P) ≤ Σ|β_F| ≤ 2M(Q) ≤ cM(T) (M[[F]] = 1), and (37) M(∂P) ≤ M(∂Q) + M(∂Q − ∂P) ≤ cM(∂Q) ≤ cM(∂T). By (21), (38) T − P = ∂R₁ + S₁ + (Q − P). Put R := R₁, S := S₁ + (Q − P). Then M(R) ≤ cM(T), M(S) ≤ cM(∂T) + cM(∂Q) ≤ cM(∂T). Supports: if β_F ≠ 0 then θ_F ≠ 0 on a set of positive measure, so F̊ meets spt Q and F ⊆ {dist(·, spt Q) ≤ √n} ⊆ {dist(·, spt T) ≤ √d + √n}; if Q⌞F̊ − β_F[[F]] ≠ 0 then θ_F is not a.e. constant (a median of a constant is that constant), so |Dθ_F|(F̊) > 0, F̊ meets spt ∂Q and F ⊆ {dist(·, spt ∂T) ≤ √d + √n}. Hence spt P ∪ spt R ⊆ {dist(·, spt T) ≤ √d + √n} and spt ∂P ∪ spt S ⊆ spt ∂Q ∪ spt(Q−P) ∪ spt S₁ ⊆ {dist(·, spt ∂T) ≤ √d + √n}; since ℓ ≥ 1, √d + √n < 2√d. Integrality: if T is integer multiplicity, Q is (C5), all θ_F are integer valued, all β_F ∈ ℤ, P is integer multiplicity (A7), R = R₁ is; if also ∂T is, S₁ is and S = S₁ + (Q − P) is (A4(c)). All constants depend only on (n,ℓ) (through β, c of Lemma 5.4 and A6). This is 5.1.

Part D — the scaled version 5.3 and the Lean conclusions.
D1. Let ρ > 0, η_ρ(x) := ρx. Apply Part C to T′ := (η_{1/ρ})_#T: M(T′) = ρ^{−n}M(T), M(∂T′) = ρ^{1−n}M(∂T), spt T′ = ρ⁻¹spt T. Get T′ − P′ = ∂R′ + S′ and push forward by η_ρ (A2(b); ∂ commutes): with Pc := η_{ρ#}P′, R := η_{ρ#}R′, S := η_{ρ#}S′ we have T − Pc = ∂R + S, i.e. ∀ω, T(ω) − Pc(ω) = R.boundary(ω) + S(ω). Masses scale by ρ^k for k-currents: M(Pc) = ρⁿM(P′) ≤ CM(T), M(∂Pc) ≤ CM(∂T), M(R) = ρ^{n+1}M(R′) ≤ CρM(T), M(S) = ρⁿM(S′) ≤ CρM(∂T). Supports scale by ρ, so spt Pc ∪ spt R ⊆ {dist(·, spt T) < 2√d·ρ} = `thickening (2√d ρ) T.support` and spt ∂Pc ∪ spt S ⊆ `thickening (2√d ρ) T.boundary.support` (if spt ∂T = ∅ then M(∂T) = 0 and ∂Pc = S = 0, so both sides are empty).
D2. η_{ρ#}[[F]] = [[ρF]] for F ∈ 𝓛_n with the same orientation e_α, so Pc = Σ_{F}β_F[[ρF]]; indexing ρ(z + F_α) by (z, α) ∈ `LatticeFaceIndex (m+1) (m+1+ℓ)` and setting β(z,α) := β_{z+F_α} gives `IsLatticeChain ρ β Pc` (A7).
D3. If T is integer multiplicity so is T′ (A4(e)); then β takes integer values and Pc, R are integer multiplicity (A4(e), A7); if also ∂T is, S is. C := C(n,ℓ) from Part C (the maximum of the constants) works for all T and ρ. This proves `DeformationTheorem`.
proof_key_steps: Tools: representation/restriction, products with [[(0,1)]], push-forwards and homotopy formula for Lipschitz maps (2.17–2.29), integer multiplicity calculus and completeness (3.2, 3.13), 2.35–2.37, Poincaré/extension with medians (Ch. 2, 2.7–2.9), lattice chains.

Consistency (A3): for integer multiplicity X and Lipschitz g with g|spt X proper, (I) the 2.29 push-forward equals the 3.6 formula S — fixed compact target neighbourhood K of spt ω; for small ε all contributing source points lie (a.e.) in the compact set g⁻¹(K) ∩ spt X; one integrable dominator θ‖ω‖Λ^k1_{g⁻¹(K)∩spt X}; weak continuity of minors on each C¹ chart piece; Tannery summation; (II) S equals the sibling 3.9 push-forward S̃, whose representation (M′,θ′,ξ′) has only a positive, locally integrable real θ′: the vector measures θξH^k⌞M and θ′ξ′H^k⌞M′ agree on bounded Borel sets; λ := H^k⌞(M ∪ M′) is σ-finite via the compact exhaustion K_j and Markov's inequality on M′ ∩ K_j ∩ {θ′ ≥ 1/r}; Radon–Nikodym uniqueness gives H^k(M Δ M′) = 0, θ = θ′, ξ = ξ′ a.e.; hence equal weighted tangent spaces, equal differentials on them and S̃ = S, so g_#X is integer multiplicity.
Lemma 5.4: radial-projection retraction ψ onto L_n off the dual skeleton L_{ℓ−1}(a), periodic, |Dψ| ≤ c/dist(·, L_{ℓ−1}(a)).
Choose a ∈ B_{1/4}(q) good for T and ∂T (covering lemma + Fubini): M(T⌞L_{ℓ−1}(a;σ)) ≤ cσ^{n+1}M(T), same for ∂T.
Choose good radii σ_ν with small slices of T (and finite slices of ∂T) via the sibling slicing theorem.

Estimates for consecutive good radii, telescoping, M-Cauchy limits Q, R₁, S₁ and the homotopy formula give T − Q = ∂R₁ + S₁ with spt Q ⊆ L_n and mass/support bounds; integrality via consistency and 3.13.
On each n-face, Q is a BV multiple of [[F]] (2.35); integer medians β_F, Poincaré/extension bounds and Q⌞L_{n−1} = 0 give P = Σβ_F[[F]] with M(Q−P), M(∂Q−∂P) ≤ cM(∂Q).
T − P = ∂R₁ + (S₁ + Q − P): mass, support and integrality conclusions of 5.1.
Scale by ρ (5.3) and translate into IsLatticeChain, thickening supports and the Lean mass bounds.

subproblems.title: Isoperimetric theorem (Simon 6.1)
subproblems.statement: For all m, ℓ ∈ ℕ with ℓ ≥ 1 there is c = c(m,ℓ) ∈ [0,∞) such that every integer multiplicity T ∈ D_{m+1}(ℝ^{m+2+ℓ}) with compact support and ∂T = 0 satisfies T = ∂R for some integer multiplicity R ∈ D_{m+2}(ℝ^{m+2+ℓ}) with compact support and M(R)^{(m+1)/(m+2)} ≤ c·M(T).
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, 6.1 (Isoperimetric Theorem) and its printed proof (pp. 168–169). Book n = m + 2 ≥ 2: T ∈ D_{n−1}(ℝ^{n+ℓ}) = D_{m+1}(ℝ^{m+2+ℓ}), ℓ ≥ 1. The printed proof: apply the scaled deformation theorem 5.3 to T at a scale ρ; S = 0 because ∂T = 0; the polyhedral part P has mass N(ρ)ρ^{n−1} with N(ρ) ∈ ℕ and M(P) ≤ cM(T), so P = 0 for ρ = (2cM(T))^{1/(n−1)}; then T = ∂R with M(R) ≤ cρM(T). It is copied below with the details filled in. Errata applied: “F ∈ F_{n−1}(ρ)” means F ∈ 𝓛_{n−1}(ρ), “since M ≤ cM(T)” means M(P) ≤ cM(T), and the printed last display M(R) ≤ cρM(T) = c′M(T)^{1/(n−1)} should read c′M(T)^{n/(n−1)} (which is equivalent to the claimed M(R)^{(n−1)/n} ≤ cM(T)).

Sibling result used: `DeformationTheorem` (5.3), applied with (m, ℓ+1): currents of degree m+1 in ℝ^{(m+1)+(ℓ+1)}; note (m+1)+(ℓ+1) = m+2+ℓ, so the ambient spaces coincide (in Lean: rewrite `Eucl (m + 1 + (ℓ + 1))` to `Eucl (m + 2 + ℓ)` by the equation m+1+(ℓ+1) = m+2+ℓ; this rewrite has been checked to typecheck).

Proof. Fix m, ℓ ≥ 1, write k := m + 1 = n − 1 ≥ 1 (degree of T), d := m + 2 + ℓ. Let C₀ = C₀(m, ℓ+1) be the constant of `DeformationTheorem` for (m, ℓ+1). Define c := (C₀(2C₀)^{1/k})^{k/(k+1)} (a constant depending only on m, ℓ; take c := 0 if C₀ = 0). Let T ∈ D_k(ℝ^d) be integer multiplicity with compact support and ∂T = 0.

1. (Finite mass.) T = τ(M,θ,ξ) with θ integrable on M ∩ K for compact K. Let χ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^d), 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 on a neighbourhood of the compact spt T, K := spt χ. For a test form ω with ‖ω‖ ≤ 1, (1 − χ)ω vanishes near spt T, so T((1−χ)ω) = 0 (a test form supported in the open zero region is annihilated: cover its compact support by finitely many open sets on which T vanishes and use a partition of unity). Hence T(ω) = ∫_M θχ⟨ω, ξ⟩dH^k ≤ ∫_{M∩K}θ dH^k, using |⟨ω,ξ⟩| ≤ |ω||ξ| and |ξ| = 1 H^k-a.e. on M (ξ = ±simpleNVector of an orthonormal frame; Cauchy–Binet). So M(T) < ∞, and M(∂T) = M(0) = 0.

2. (Trivial case.) If M(T) = 0 then |T(ω)| ≤ M(T)‖ω‖ = 0 for all ω, so T = 0; take R := 0 (integer multiplicity with M = ∅, spt R = ∅ compact, ∂R = 0 = T, M(R)^{k/(k+1)} = 0 ≤ c·0). Assume from now on 0 < M(T) < ∞.

3. (Deformation.) Put ρ := (2C₀M(T))^{1/k} if C₀ > 0 (if C₀ = 0, take ρ := 1). By `DeformationTheorem` (with m, ℓ+1, after the dimension rewrite) there are β, Pc = Σ_F β_F[[F]] (F ∈ 𝓛_k(ρ), `IsLatticeChain ρ β Pc`), R ∈ D_{k+1}(ℝ^d), S ∈ D_k(ℝ^d) with T − Pc = ∂R + S, M(Pc) ≤ C₀M(T), M(R) ≤ C₀ρM(T), M(S) ≤ C₀ρM(∂T) = 0, spt Pc ∪ spt R ⊆ {dist(·, spt T) < 2√d·ρ}; and since T is integer multiplicity, all β_F ∈ ℤ and Pc, R are integer multiplicity.

4. (S = 0.) M(S) = 0, so S = 0 (Step 2's argument).

5. (Pc = 0; printed (1) “M(P) = N(ρ)ρ^{n−1}”.) Claim: if some β_{F₀} ≠ 0 then M(Pc) ≥ |β_{F₀}|ρ^k. Let F₀ = ρ(z + F_α) and K₀ a compact subset of the relative interior F̊₀. Take ω := s·φ·dx^α with s := sign(β_{F₀}), φ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^d), 0 ≤ φ ≤ 1, φ = 1 on K₀, and spt φ disjoint from every face F ≠ F₀ with the same direction α (possible: such faces are closed and at positive distance from the compact K₀ ⊆ F̊₀ — those in the same affine k-plane meet F₀ only in its relative boundary, those in parallel planes are at distance ≥ ρ — and only finitely many of them meet a bounded neighbourhood of K₀). Then |ω| ≤ 1 (|dx^α| = 1), and for faces F with direction α′ ≠ α, [[F]](ω) = ∫_F sφ dx^α(e_{α′}) dH^k = 0 (dx^α(e_{α′}) = 0). Hence Pc(ω) = Σ_F β_F[[F]](ω) = |β_{F₀}|∫_{F₀}φ dH^k ≥ |β_{F₀}|H^k(K₀) (φ = 1 on K₀, φ ≥ 0), and Pc(ω) ≤ M(Pc) since ω is mass-admissible. Letting K₀ ↑ F̊₀ gives M(Pc) ≥ |β_{F₀}|H^k(F₀) = |β_{F₀}|ρ^k. If C₀ > 0, M(Pc) ≤ C₀M(T) = ρ^k/2 < ρ^k, so no β_F ∈ ℤ∖{0} occurs; if C₀ = 0, M(Pc) = 0 and again all β_F = 0. Thus Pc = 0.

6. (Conclusion.) From Steps 3–5, T = ∂R (as functionals on test forms, hence `R.boundary = T` by extensionality). R is integer multiplicity. spt R ⊆ {dist(·, spt T) < 2√d ρ} is bounded (spt T compact) and closed (spt R = ℝ^d ∖ zeroRegion, zeroRegion open), hence compact. Finally M(R) ≤ C₀ρM(T) = C₀(2C₀)^{1/k}M(T)^{(k+1)/k}, so M(R)^{k/(k+1)} ≤ (C₀(2C₀)^{1/k})^{k/(k+1)}M(T) = cM(T) (rpow in [0,∞] is monotone; exponent k/(k+1) = (m+1)/(m+2) > 0). If C₀ = 0 then M(R) = 0 and the inequality is trivial. This proves `IsoperimetricTheorem`.
proof_key_steps: T has finite mass (integer multiplicity, compact support); T = 0 is trivial.
Apply the sibling deformation theorem with (m, ℓ+1) after rewriting m+1+(ℓ+1) = m+2+ℓ, at scale ρ = (2C₀M(T))^{1/(m+1)}.
S = 0 because M(S) ≤ C₀ρM(∂T) = 0.
A nonzero integer lattice chain has mass ≥ ρ^{m+1} (test forms ±φdx^α near one face), while M(Pc) ≤ ρ^{m+1}/2; so Pc = 0.
Hence T = ∂R with R integer multiplicity, spt R closed and within 2√d ρ of spt T (compact).
M(R) ≤ C₀ρM(T) = C₀(2C₀)^{1/(m+1)}M(T)^{(m+2)/(m+1)} gives the isoperimetric inequality.

subproblems.title: Weak polyhedral approximation theorem (Simon 6.2)
subproblems.statement: For all m, ℓ ∈ ℕ with ℓ ≥ 1, every open U ⊆ ℝ^{m+1+ℓ} and every integer multiplicity T ∈ D_{m+1}(U) with M_W(T) < ∞ and M_W(∂T) < ∞ for all W ⊂⊂ U, there are ρ : ℕ → (0,∞) antitone with ρ_k → 0, integer coefficients β_k on the faces 𝓛_{m+1}(ρ_k) and currents P_k ∈ D_{m+1}(U) with IsLatticeChain ρ_k β_k P_k for all k and P_k ⇀ T in U.
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, 6.2 (Weak Polyhedral Approximation Theorem) and its printed proof (pp. 169–170). Book n = m + 1, ambient ℝ^{n+ℓ}, ℓ ≥ 1. The printed proof: first the case U = ℝ^{n+ℓ}, M(T), M(∂T) < ∞ via the scaled deformation theorem with ρ = ρ_k ↓ 0; then the general case via T_λ = T ⌞ {φ > λ} for an exhaustion function φ and a.e. λ (4.5), and a diagonal choice λ_j ↓ 0. It is copied below with the details filled in. Errata applied: “F ∈ F_n(ρ_k)”, “β_R^{(k)}” mean F ∈ 𝓛_n(ρ_k), β_F^{(k)} (README); “Pk(ω) → Tk(ω)” means P_k(ω) → T(ω); “{x D φ(x) > λ}” means {x : φ(x) > λ}; we use T⌞{φ ≥ λ} instead of T⌞{φ > λ}, which avoids discarding the countably many λ with μ_T({φ = λ}) > 0 (the two coincide for all other λ).

Sibling results used: `DeformationTheorem` (5.3) and `SlicingTheorem` (§4).

Setting. n := m + 1, d := n + ℓ, U ⊆ ℝ^d open, T ∈ D_n(U) integer multiplicity with M_W(T), M_W(∂T) < ∞ for all W ⊂⊂ U.

Preliminaries. (P1) Representation and restriction (Simon 2.7–2.9): T and ∂T have locally finite mass, so T(ω) = ∫⟨ω,T⃗⟩dμ_T, ∂T(ω) = ∫⟨ω,∂T⃗⟩dμ_{∂T} with Radon μ_T, μ_{∂T} on U, unit vector fields, μ(W) = M_W for open W ⊆ U; X⌞A(ω) := ∫_A⟨ω,X⃗⟩dμ_X is the unique restriction (`IsRestriction`), M_W(X⌞A) = μ_X(W∩A), and |X(ω)| ≤ M_W(X)‖ω‖ for tsupport ω ⊆ W. (P2) Restriction of an integer multiplicity current τ(M,θ,ξ) to a Borel set A is τ(M∩A,θ,ξ), integer multiplicity (at Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M∩A the measure θHⁿ⌞(M∖A) has zero density — apply Ch. 1, 3.6 to the finite measures θHⁿ⌞((M∖A) ∩ B) for balls B ⊂⊂ U — so the weighted tangent spaces agree). (P3) Extension: if X ∈ D_k(U) has compact support K ⊆ U, put X̃(ω) := X(χω) for ω ∈ D^k(ℝ^d), with χ ∈ C_c^∞(U), 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 near K (independent of χ since X kills forms vanishing near spt X); X̃ ∈ D_k(ℝ^d), ∂X̃ = (∂X)~, M(X̃) = M(X) (= M_W(X) for any open W ⊇ K, W ⊆ U), M(∂X̃) = M(∂X), X̃(ω) = X(ω) for ω ∈ D^k(U), and X̃ is integer multiplicity if X is (same triple, Hⁿ(M∖K) = 0). (P4) The restriction to U of a current Y ∈ D_k(ℝ^d), Y|_U(ω) := Y(ω) for ω ∈ D^k(U) ⊆ D^k(ℝ^d), is in D_k(U); if `IsLatticeChain ρ β Y` (on ℝ^d) then `IsLatticeChain ρ β (Y|_U)`.

Proof.

1. (Exhaustion function.) If U = ℝ^d let φ(x) := 1/(1+|x|); otherwise let φ(x) := min{dist(x, ℝ^d∖U), 1/(1+|x|)}. (If U = ∅ then T = 0 and P_k := 0 with β := 0, ρ_k := 1/(k+1) work; assume U ≠ ∅.) φ is Lipschitz with constant 1, φ > 0 on U, φ = 0 off U, and for λ > 0, {φ ≥ λ} ⊆ {x : dist(x,ℝ^d∖U) ≥ λ, |x| ≤ 1/λ} is compact and contained in U; in particular W_λ := {φ > λ/2} is open with compact closure in U ({φ ≥ λ/2}), i.e. W_λ ⊂⊂ U.

2. (Slices; 4.5 via the sibling theorem.) Apply `SlicingTheorem` to T, f = φ, L = 1 on U: we get S_t ∈ D_m(U) with `IsSlice T φ t S_t`, i.e. ∂(T⌞{φ < t}) = S_t + (∂T)⌞{φ < t} (sets intersected with U; P1 identifies the restrictions), spt S_t ⊆ spt T ∩ {φ = t}, and the mass bound. For k ≥ 1 apply the mass bound with W := W_{1/(k+1)} (open ⊆ U), L_W := 1 (|Dφ| ≤ 1 a.e.), a := 1/(k+1), b := 1/k and R := T⌞{a < φ < b}: there is a measurable g_k ≥ M_W(S_t) on (a,b) with ∫_a^b g_k ≤ M_W(R) = μ_T(W ∩ {a < φ < b}) ≤ μ_T({φ ≥ 1/(k+1)}) < ∞. Hence M_W(S_t) < ∞ for a.e. t ∈ (1/(k+1), 1/k). For such t, spt S_t ⊆ {φ = t} is a compact subset of W, so M(S_t) = M_W(S_t) < ∞ (a test form ω with ‖ω‖ ≤ 1 satisfies S_t(ω) = S_t(χω) with χ ∈ C_c^∞(W), 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 near spt S_t). Doing this for all k, M(S_λ) < ∞ for a.e. λ ∈ (0,1).

3. (The truncated currents T′_λ.) For such λ let A_λ := {x ∈ U : φ(x) ≥ λ} and T′_λ := T⌞A_λ = T − T⌞{φ < λ}. Then T′_λ is integer multiplicity (P2), spt T′_λ ⊆ A_λ compact ⊆ U, M(T′_λ) ≤ μ_T(A_λ) < ∞, and ∂T′_λ = ∂T − ∂(T⌞{φ<λ}) = (∂T)⌞A_λ − S_λ, so M(∂T′_λ) ≤ μ_{∂T}(A_λ) + M(S_λ) < ∞. Moreover T′_λ(ω) = T(ω) whenever φ ≥ λ on tsupport ω, because then the integrand ⟨ω,T⃗⟩·1_{φ<λ} of T⌞{φ<λ}(ω) vanishes identically.

4. (Case of finite mass in ℝ^d — the printed first paragraph.) For X ∈ D_n(ℝ^d) integer multiplicity with M(X) + M(∂X) < ∞ and ρ > 0, `DeformationTheorem` gives integer valued β, Pc = Σβ_F[[F]] with `IsLatticeChain ρ β Pc`, and R, S with X − Pc = ∂R + S, M(R) ≤ CρM(X), M(S) ≤ CρM(∂X). Hence for every ω ∈ D^n(ℝ^d): |X(ω) − Pc(ω)| = |R(dω) + S(ω)| ≤ M(R)‖dω‖ + M(S)‖ω‖ ≤ Cρ(M(X)‖dω‖ + M(∂X)‖ω‖) (printed (1),(2)).

5. (Diagonal choice — the printed last paragraph.) Index by k ∈ ℕ = {0,1,2,…}. Choose λ_k ↓ 0 (k ≥ 0) with λ_k ∈ (0,1) admissible in Step 2 (possible since admissible λ form a full-measure subset of (0,1)), and let X_k := (T′_{λ_k})~ ∈ D_n(ℝ^d) (P3): integer multiplicity, M(X_k) + M(∂X_k) < ∞. Define ρ_k := min{ρ_{k−1}, 1/((k+1)(1 + M(X_k) + M(∂X_k)))} for k ≥ 1 and ρ₀ := 1/(1 + M(X₀) + M(∂X₀)). Then ρ_k > 0 for all k ∈ ℕ, ρ is antitone and ρ_k → 0. By Step 4 with X = X_k, ρ = ρ_k obtain integer valued β_k and Pc_k with `IsLatticeChain ρ_k β_k Pc_k` and |X_k(ω) − Pc_k(ω)| ≤ (C/(k+1))(‖dω‖ + ‖ω‖) for ω ∈ D^n(ℝ^d). Let P_k := Pc_k|_U (P4): `IsLatticeChain (ρ k) (fun F => (β k F : ℝ)) (P_k)` for every k ∈ ℕ.

6. (Weak convergence.) Let ω ∈ D^n(U). K := tsupport ω is compact ⊆ U, so φ ≥ δ > 0 on K. For k with λ_k < δ, X_k(ω) = T′_{λ_k}(ω) = T(ω) (P3 and Step 3). Hence |P_k(ω) − T(ω)| = |Pc_k(ω) − X_k(ω)| ≤ (C/(k+1))(‖dω‖ + ‖ω‖) → 0. So `WeaklyConvergesOn P T`, and (ρ, β, P) witness `PolyhedralApproximation`. (In the special case U = ℝ^d with M(T), M(∂T) < ∞ one may take X_k = T directly, which is the printed first paragraph.)
proof_key_steps: Lipschitz exhaustion function φ with {φ ≥ λ} compact in U.
Sibling slicing theorem: for a.e. λ ∈ (0,1) the slice ⟨T,φ,λ⟩ has finite mass.
T′_λ := T⌞{φ ≥ λ} is integer multiplicity with compact support and finite mass and boundary mass; extend to ℝ^{m+1+ℓ}.
Sibling deformation theorem at scale ρ: |X(ω) − Pc(ω)| ≤ Cρ(M(X)‖dω‖ + M(∂X)‖ω‖).
Diagonal choice λ_k ↓ 0, antitone ρ_k → 0 small relative to the masses; restrict the lattice chains to U.
For each test form, T′_{λ_k}(ω) = T(ω) eventually, so P_k(ω) → T(ω).

subproblems.title: Boundary rectifiability theorem (Simon 6.3)
subproblems.statement: For all P, m ∈ ℕ, every open U ⊆ ℝ^P and every integer multiplicity T ∈ D_{m+1}(U) with M_W(∂T) < ∞ for every open W ⊂⊂ U, the boundary ∂T ∈ D_m(U) is integer multiplicity.
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, 6.3 (Boundary Rectifiability Theorem) and its printed proof “A direct consequence of 6.2 above and the Compactness 3.11”, Remark 6.4 (“only the case ∂T_j = 0 ∀j of 3.11 is needed in the above proof”), the introduction to §6 (“in the case k = 0 this has already been established in 3.14”), the proof of 6.2 (approximation by the deformation theorem with the mass bounds M(P_k) ≤ cM(T), M(∂P_k) ≤ cM(∂T)), the printed steps (27)–(37) of the proof of 5.1, and the base case n = 0 of the induction in the proof of 8.2 (“the theorem is trivial in case n = 0”). Book n = m + 1. The printed argument is: approximate T (localized so that it has finite mass and boundary mass) by integer polyhedral chains P_k as in the proof of 6.2, with P_k ⇀ T and sup_k M(∂P_k) < ∞; then ∂P_k are integer multiplicity cycles of bounded mass converging weakly to ∂T, so ∂T is integer multiplicity by 3.11 in the case of zero boundaries, i.e. by 8.2 (Remark 6.4 shows this is not circular). It is written out below, with these points made explicit for the Lean statement (general ambient dimension P): (a) the mass bounds needed are those of the deformation theorem, not of the statement `PolyhedralApproximation` (which records no mass bounds), so the deformation theorem is invoked directly as in the printed proof of 6.2; (b) localization by slicing and a patching lemma replace the printed “U = ℝ^{n+ℓ} first” reduction; (c) when P = m + 1 (book k = 0) the polyhedral approximation is provided by the printed steps (27)–(37) of the proof of 5.1 with Q = T (the retraction ψ is the identity because L_n = ℝⁿ); (d) when m = 0 the case “n = 0” of the compactness theorem (trivial, as printed in 8.2) is written out. Erratum applied: the hypothesis printed “M(∂T) < ∞ ∀W ⊂⊂ U” means M_W(∂T) < ∞ (README).

Sibling results used: `DeformationTheorem` (5.3), `SlicingTheorem` (§4), `IntegralityOfWeakLimits` (8.2).

Setting. U ⊆ ℝ^P open, T ∈ D_{m+1}(U) integer multiplicity, M_W(∂T) < ∞ for all W ⊂⊂ U. Write n := m + 1. Being integer multiplicity, T has locally finite mass (M_W(T) ≤ ∫_{M∩closure W}θ dHⁿ < ∞).

Preliminaries.
(P1) Representation, restriction (Simon 2.7–2.9): currents X of locally finite mass satisfy X(ω) = ∫⟨ω,X⃗⟩dμ_X, μ_X(W) = M_W(X) for open W, X⌞A(ω) := ∫_A⟨ω,X⃗⟩dμ_X is the unique restriction, M_W(X⌞A) = μ_X(W∩A), |X(ω)| ≤ M_W(X)‖ω‖ if tsupport ω ⊆ W, and M(X) = 0 ⇒ X = 0. If X vanishes on an open set V, then μ_X(V) = 0.
(P2) Restriction of an integer multiplicity current to a Borel set is integer multiplicity (τ(M,θ,ξ)⌞A = τ(M∩A,θ,ξ); weighted tangent spaces agree a.e. by the density theorem Ch. 1, 3.6).
(P3) Extension/restriction of domains: a current X ∈ D_k(U) with compact support in U extends to X̃ ∈ D_k(ℝ^P) (X̃(ω) := X(χω), χ ∈ C_c^∞(U), 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 near spt X; independent of χ because X annihilates test forms vanishing near spt X), with ∂X̃ = (∂X)~, the same masses, X̃ = X on D^k(U), integer multiplicity preserved; conversely Y ∈ D_k(ℝ^P) restricts to Y|_U ∈ D_k(U), and if Y = τ(M,θ,ξ) then Y|_U = τ(M∩U,θ,ξ) is integer multiplicity (the weighted tangent space at x ∈ U only depends on M, θ near x).
(P4) Integer lattice chains. For β : 𝓛_k(ρ) → ℤ, Σβ_F[[F]] is integer multiplicity (disjoint relative interiors, Hᵏ-null relative boundaries, local finiteness). By Stokes' theorem on a cube (Fubini and the fundamental theorem of calculus), ∂[[F]] = Σ_{i=1}^{k}(−1)^{i−1}([[F_i⁺]] − [[F_i⁻]]) for the (k−1)-faces F_i^± of F (for k = 1: ∂[[F]] = δ_{end} − δ_{start}). Hence the boundary of an integer lattice k-chain is an integer lattice (k−1)-chain, hence integer multiplicity, and its boundary is 0.
(P5) Patching lemma. Let X ∈ D_k(U). Suppose every x ∈ U has an open neighbourhood V_x ⊆ U and an integer multiplicity Y_x ∈ D_k(U) with X(ω) = Y_x(ω) whenever tsupport ω ⊆ V_x. Then X is integer multiplicity. Proof: by Lindelöf choose x_i with U = ⋃_iV_i (V_i := V_{x_i}), Y_i = τ(M_i,θ_i,ξ_i). (i) For all i, i′ the currents Y_i, Y_{i′} agree on test forms supported in V_i ∩ V_{i′}, so the ℝ^{#I(k,P)}-valued (I(k,P) = the strictly increasing k-tuples in {1,…,P}) Radon measures θ_iξ_iHᵏ⌞M_i and θ_{i′}ξ_{i′}Hᵏ⌞M_{i′} coincide on V_i ∩ V_{i′}; taking total variations (|ξ| = 1 a.e.), θ_iHᵏ⌞M_i = θ_{i′}Hᵏ⌞M_{i′} there, so Hᵏ((M_i Δ M_{i′}) ∩ V_i ∩ V_{i′}) = 0 (θ > 0), θ_i = θ_{i′} and ξ_i = ξ_{i′} Hᵏ-a.e. on M_i ∩ M_{i′} ∩ V_i ∩ V_{i′} (Radon–Nikodym uniqueness with respect to Hᵏ⌞(M_i ∪ M_{i′}), which is σ-finite, indeed locally finite in U, because θ_i, θ_{i′} take values in {1,2,…} and are integrable on compact subsets of U). (ii) Let D_i := V_i ∖ ⋃_{j<i}V_j (disjoint Borel sets covering U), M := ⋃_i(M_i ∩ D_i), θ := θ_i and ξ := ξ_i on M_i ∩ D_i. (iii) X = τ(M,θ,ξ): for a test form ω choose finitely many V_1,…,V_I covering tsupport ω and χ_i ∈ C_c^∞(V_i) with Σχ_i = 1 on tsupport ω; then X(ω) = Σ_iY_i(χ_iω) = Σ_i∫_{M_i}θ_iχ_i⟨ω,ξ_i⟩dHᵏ = Σ_i∫_Mθχ_i⟨ω,ξ⟩dHᵏ = ∫_Mθ⟨ω,ξ⟩dHᵏ, using (i) on each V_i ∩ D_j (the D_j partition U, D_j ⊆ V_j, and on V_i ∩ D_j the triple (M,θ,ξ) = (M_j,θ_j,ξ_j) agrees with (M_i,θ_i,ξ_i) up to Hᵏ-null sets). (iv) `IsRectifiableTriple U k M θ ξ`: M ⊆ U, Hᵏ-measurable, countably k-rectifiable (countable union of subsets of rectifiable sets); θ ∈ {1,2,…}; for compact K ⊆ U, K ⊆ V_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ V_I for some I, so K ∩ D_j = ∅ for j > I and ∫_{M∩K}θ = Σ_{j≤I}∫_{M_j∩D_j∩K}θ_j < ∞; ξ is measurable; by (i), (M,θ) agrees with (M_i,θ_i) on V_i up to Hᵏ-null sets, and the weighted approximate tangent space at x ∈ V_i depends only on M ∩ V_i and θ|V_i modulo Hᵏ-null sets (for small r the blow-up integrals only see x + r·spt f ⊆ V_i, and Hᵏ(η_{x,r}Z) = r^{−k}Hᵏ(Z) = 0 for null Z), so the `orients` property of Y_i transfers to (M,θ,ξ) at Hᵏ-a.e. x ∈ M ∩ D_i.
(P6) The case n = 0 of the compactness theorem (printed: trivial). Let X_j ∈ D_0(U′) (U′ ⊆ ℝ^P open) be integer multiplicity with sup_j M_W(X_j) < ∞ for all W ⊂⊂ U′, and X_j ⇀ X. Then X is integer multiplicity. Proof: a 0-dimensional integer multiplicity current is X_j(φ) = Σ_{x∈M_j}c_j(x)φ(x) with M_j locally finite (countable, H⁰ = counting measure, θ_j ≥ 1 locally summable) and c_j = θ_jξ_j ∈ ℤ∖{0} (simple 0-vectors are ±1); M_W(X_j) = Σ_{x∈M_j∩W}|c_j(x)| (test with bumps of the right sign). Fix W ⊂⊂ U′ and C ≥ sup_jM_W(X_j). Then M_j ∩ W has at most C points; pass to a subsequence along which #(M_j ∩ W) = N is constant, the points x_{j,1},…,x_{j,N} converge to x_1,…,x_N ∈ closure(W), and the coefficients c_j(x_{j,i}) (integers bounded by C) are constant = a_i. For φ ∈ C_c^∞(W), X_j(φ) = Σ_ia_iφ(x_{j,i}) → Σ_ia_iφ(x_i) (φ = 0 on ∂W), so X(φ) = Σ_{y∈W}c(y)φ(y) with c(y) := Σ_{i : x_i = y}a_i ∈ ℤ. Using an exhaustion W_1 ⊆ W_2 ⊆ … of U′ and the fact that the coefficients of a finite sum of Dirac masses are determined by the functional, these representations are compatible, so X = Σ_{y∈D}c(y)δ_y with D := {c ≠ 0} locally finite in U′. Hence X = τ(D, |c|, sign c): D is countable (countably 0-rectifiable, H⁰-measurable), |c| ∈ {1,2,…} is locally summable, sign c = ±simpleNVector(∅), and the weighted tangent space at each isolated point of D is {0} = span ∅.
(P7) Polyhedral approximation with mass bounds. Let X ∈ D_n(ℝ^P) be integer multiplicity with M(X) + M(∂X) < ∞, and ρ > 0. Then there are integer lattice chains Pc_ρ = Σ_{F∈𝓛_n(ρ)}β_F[[F]] (β_F ∈ ℤ) with M(∂Pc_ρ) ≤ C·M(∂X) and |X(ω) − Pc_ρ(ω)| ≤ Cρ(M(X)‖dω‖ + M(∂X)‖ω‖) for all ω ∈ Dⁿ(ℝ^P), C independent of ρ:
 – if P ≥ n + 1, write ℓ := P − n ≥ 1 (so `Eucl P` = `Eucl (m+1+ℓ)` after rewriting P = m+1+ℓ) and apply `DeformationTheorem`: X − Pc = ∂R + S with M(∂Pc) ≤ CM(∂X), M(R) ≤ CρM(X), M(S) ≤ CρM(∂X), β integer valued; then |X(ω) − Pc(ω)| ≤ M(R)‖dω‖ + M(S)‖ω‖;
 – if P = n (book k = 0), use the printed steps (27)–(37) of the proof of 5.1 with Q := X: by Simon 2.35, X(a dx¹∧⋯∧dxⁿ) = ∫aθ dLⁿ with θ ∈ BV(ℝⁿ) integer valued (X integer multiplicity), M(X) = ∫|θ|, M(∂X) = |Dθ|(ℝⁿ); θLⁿ does not charge the (n−1)-skeleton of 𝓛_n(ρ), so X = Σ_{F}(θ1_{F̊})[[ℝⁿ]]; choose for each cube F ∈ 𝓛_n(ρ) an integer median β_F of θ on F̊ (31) and let Pc := Σβ_F[[F]]; by Ch. 2, 2.7 and 2.9 rescaled to cubes of side ρ (32), ∫_{F̊}|θ − β_F| ≤ cρ|Dθ|(F̊) and |D((θ−β_F)1_{F̊})|(ℝⁿ) ≤ c|Dθ|(F̊); summing over F (34),(37): M(X − Pc) ≤ cρM(∂X) and M(∂Pc) ≤ M(∂X) + M(∂(X − Pc)) ≤ (1+c)M(∂X); so |X(ω) − Pc(ω)| ≤ cρM(∂X)‖ω‖.

Proof.

1. (Trivial dimensions.) If P < n, every n-covector on ℝ^P is 0, so Dⁿ(U) = {0} and ∂T(ω) = T(dω) = T(0) = 0 for all ω; ∂T = 0 is integer multiplicity (M = ∅). Assume P ≥ n.

2. (Localization by slicing; printed 4.5 as used in 6.2.) Fix x₀ ∈ U and r₀ > 0 with B̄_{2r₀}(x₀) ⊆ U. Apply `SlicingTheorem` to T (locally finite mass and boundary mass), f := |· − x₀| (1-Lipschitz), with W := B_{2r₀}(x₀), L_W := 1, (a,b) := (r₀/2, r₀), R := T⌞{r₀/2 < f < r₀}: the slices S_r (`IsSlice T f r S_r`, i.e. ∂(T⌞B_r(x₀)) = S_r + (∂T)⌞B_r(x₀)) satisfy M_W(S_r) ≤ g(r) with ∫_{r₀/2}^{r₀}g ≤ μ_T(B_{r₀}(x₀)) < ∞, so M_W(S_r) < ∞ for a.e. r ∈ (r₀/2, r₀); since spt S_r ⊆ ∂B_r(x₀) ⊆ W is compact, M(S_r) = M_W(S_r) < ∞ for such r. Fix such an r.

3. (The localized current.) T′ := T⌞B_r(x₀) is integer multiplicity (P2), spt T′ ⊆ B̄_r(x₀) (compact ⊆ U), M(T′) ≤ μ_T(B_r(x₀)) < ∞ and M(∂T′) ≤ M(S_r) + μ_{∂T}(B_r(x₀)) < ∞. Let X := T̃′ ∈ D_n(ℝ^P) (P3): integer multiplicity, M(X) + M(∂X) < ∞, and X(η) = T(η) for every η ∈ Dⁿ(U) with tsupport η ⊆ B_r(x₀).

4. (Approximation — printed proof of 6.2, first paragraph.) For k ≥ 1 let Pc_k := Pc_{1/k} from (P7). Then for ω ∈ D^m(ℝ^P): |∂X(ω) − ∂Pc_k(ω)| = |X(dω) − Pc_k(dω)| ≤ (C/k)(M(X)‖ddω‖ + M(∂X)‖dω‖) = (C/k)M(∂X)‖dω‖ → 0, i.e. ∂Pc_k ⇀ ∂X in ℝ^P; and M(∂Pc_k) ≤ CM(∂X) for all k. By (P4) each Y_k := ∂Pc_k is integer multiplicity with ∂Y_k = 0 (when m ≥ 1).

5. (Compactness for cycles — 3.11 with ∂T_j = 0, Remark 6.4.) If m ≥ 1, write m = m′ + 1; then Y_k ∈ D_{m′+1}(ℝ^P) satisfy `IsIntegralCurrent` (Y_k and ∂Y_k = 0 are integer multiplicity), sup_k(M_W(Y_k) + M_W(∂Y_k)) ≤ CM(∂X) < ∞ for every W, and Y_k ⇀ ∂X; by `IntegralityOfWeakLimits` (with P, m′, U = ℝ^P), ∂X is integer multiplicity. If m = 0, the Y_k are integer multiplicity 0-currents with M(Y_k) ≤ CM(∂X) converging weakly to ∂X, so ∂X is integer multiplicity by (P6).

6. (Local agreement.) Let Z := (∂X)|_U ∈ D_m(U) (P3), integer multiplicity. For ω ∈ D^m(U) with tsupport ω ⊆ B_r(x₀): ∂T(ω) = T(dω) = X(dω) = ∂X(ω) = Z(ω) (Step 3, tsupport dω ⊆ B_r(x₀)). So ∂T agrees on the open neighbourhood V_{x₀} := B_r(x₀) of x₀ with an integer multiplicity current in D_m(U).

7. (Patching.) Since x₀ ∈ U was arbitrary, (P5) applied to X := ∂T (k = m) shows that ∂T is integer multiplicity. This proves `BoundaryRectifiability`.
proof_key_steps: If P < m+1 all (m+1)-forms vanish and ∂T = 0.
Localize: by the sibling slicing theorem, for a.e. small r, T⌞B_r(x₀) is integer multiplicity with finite mass and boundary mass; extend to ℝ^P.
Polyhedral approximation with mass bounds: sibling deformation theorem (P ≥ m+2) or printed steps (27)–(37) of 5.1 with Q = T (P = m+1); ∂P_k ⇀ ∂X and sup M(∂P_k) < ∞.
∂P_k are integer lattice cycles (Stokes on cubes).
Compactness for cycles (Remark 6.4): sibling 8.2 for m ≥ 1, the n = 0 case (finitely many integer Dirac masses) for m = 0; so ∂X is integer multiplicity.
∂T agrees with ∂X near x₀; the patching lemma gives ∂T integer multiplicity.

subproblems.title: Flat convergence iff weak convergence (Simon 7.2)
subproblems.statement: For all P, m ∈ ℕ, every open U ⊆ ℝ^P and integer multiplicity T, T_j ∈ D_{m+1}(U) with sup_j (M_W(T_j) + M_W(∂T_j)) < ∞ for every open W ⊂⊂ U: T_j ⇀ T in U if and only if flatDistance W (T_j) T → 0 for every open W ⊂⊂ U, where d_W(X,Y) = inf{M_W(S) + M_W(R) : X − Y = ∂R + S, R ∈ D_{m+2}(U), S ∈ D_{m+1}(U) integer multiplicity}.
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, §7: definition 7.1, Theorem 7.2 and its printed proof (pp. 170–172), which uses the deformation theorem (5.3; total boundedness (1)–(3)), the localization “by 4.5(1),(2) and an argument as in 6.7(2) of Ch. 2” ((4)), and 3.13 (the series R^{(ℓ)}, S^{(ℓ)}). Book n = m + 1. The printed proof is copied below in numbered form. Points filled in for the exact Lean statement: (a) the integrality of the S produced by the deformation theorem requires ∂T integer multiplicity, which holds by 6.3 for every T in the class I of 7.1 (footnote 2 to 5.1: “if M(∂T) < ∞ then ∂T is automatically integer multiplicity if T is — see 6.3”); (b) the printed reduction (4) to currents supported in a fixed W̄ requires that the localized currents converge weakly to the localized limit, which is proved below (Step 4) for almost every localization level after passing to a subsequence; (c) the pigeonhole form of the total boundedness, which is what makes the R_r, S_r in (5) of small global mass with support in W̃; (d) for P = m + 1 (book ℓ = 0) the deformation theorem is replaced by the printed steps (27)–(37) of the proof of 5.1 with Q = T (the retraction is the identity, R = 0); for P ≤ m all currents vanish. Errata applied: in (1) the printed “Σ_{j=1}^N B_{ε,W̃}(P_j)” means the union ⋃_{j=1}^N B_{ε,W̃}(P_j); in the last paragraph “T − T_{j_ℓ}” is used with the sign convention of the Lean `flatDistance W (Tj j) T`, which concerns T_j − T = ∂R + S (replace R, S by −R, −S; negatives of integer multiplicity currents are integer multiplicity).

Sibling results used: `DeformationTheorem` (5.3), `SlicingTheorem` (§4), `BoundaryRectifiability` (6.3).

Setting. U ⊆ ℝ^P open, T, T_j ∈ D_n(U) (n = m+1) integer multiplicity, B_W := sup_j(M_W(T_j) + M_W(∂T_j)) < ∞ for all W ⊂⊂ U. d_W(X,Y) := `flatDistance W X Y` = inf{M_W(S) + M_W(R) : R ∈ D_{n+1}(U), S ∈ D_n(U) integer multiplicity, X − Y = ∂R + S}.

Preliminaries. (P1) Representation and restriction (Simon 2.7–2.9): currents of locally finite mass are X(ω) = ∫⟨ω,X⃗⟩dμ_X with μ_X(W) = M_W(X) (W open), X⌞A(ω) := ∫_A⟨ω,X⃗⟩dμ_X, M_W(X⌞A) = μ_X(W∩A), |X(ω)| ≤ M_W(X)‖ω‖ for tsupport ω ⊆ W. Mass is lower semicontinuous under weak convergence (2.14). (P2) Integer multiplicity calculus (3.2(1), 3.13): restrictions to Borel sets, integer linear combinations and M-limits (in particular M-absolutely convergent series) of integer multiplicity currents are integer multiplicity; 0 is integer multiplicity. (P3) Extension and restriction of domains: if X ∈ D_k(U) has compact support K ⊆ U, X̃(ω) := X(χω) for ω ∈ D^k(ℝ^P), with χ ∈ C_c^∞(U), 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 on a neighbourhood of K, defines X̃ ∈ D_k(ℝ^P) independent of χ (X annihilates test forms vanishing near spt X); ∂X̃ = (∂X)~, M(X̃) = M(X), spt X̃ = spt X, X̃ = X on D^k(U), and X̃ = τ(M∩K,θ,ξ) is integer multiplicity if X = τ(M,θ,ξ) is (Hᵏ(M∖spt X) = 0). Conversely Y ∈ D_k(ℝ^P) restricts to Y|_U(ω) := Y(ω), ω ∈ D^k(U); Y|_U = τ(M∩U,θ,ξ) is integer multiplicity if Y is, M_W(Y|_U) = M_W(Y) for W ⊆ U, and ∂(Y|_U) = (∂Y)|_U. (P4) Integer lattice chains Σ_{F∈𝓛_n(ρ)}β_F[[F]] (β_F ∈ ℤ) are integer multiplicity with mass Σ|β_F|ρⁿ (test with forms ±φdx^α near the relative interior of a face; faces of other directions are annihilated). (P5) Approximation with control (P ≥ n): for X ∈ D_n(ℝ^P) integer multiplicity with ∂X integer multiplicity, M(X) + M(∂X) ≤ M₀, spt X ⊆ K compact, and ρ > 0, there are an integer lattice chain Pc = Σ_{F∈𝓛_n(ρ)}β_F[[F]] and integer multiplicity R, S with X − Pc = ∂R + S, M(Pc) ≤ CM₀, M(R) + M(S) ≤ CρM₀, and spt Pc ∪ spt R ∪ spt S ⊆ {dist(·,K) < 2√P ρ}: if P ≥ n+1 this is `DeformationTheorem` with ℓ := P − n ≥ 1 (after rewriting P = m+1+ℓ); if P = n it is the printed (27)–(37) of the proof of 5.1 with Q := X (2.35 gives X = θ[[ℝⁿ]] with θ ∈ BV integer valued; β_F := integer medians of θ on the cubes F ∈ 𝓛_n(ρ), Pc := Σβ_F[[F]], R := 0, S := X − Pc = Σ_F(θ−β_F)1_{F̊}[[ℝⁿ]] integer multiplicity, M(S) ≤ cρM(∂X) by Ch. 2, 2.7, M(Pc) ≤ 2M(X); β_F ≠ 0 or (θ − β_F)1_{F̊} ≠ 0 forces F̊ ∩ spt X ≠ ∅, so the supports lie within √n·ρ of K).

Proof.

0. (Trivial dimensions.) If P < n, every n- and (n+1)-covector on ℝ^P vanishes, all currents in the statement are 0, d_W(T_j,T) ≤ M_W(0) + M_W(0) = 0 (take R = S = 0), and both sides of the equivalence hold. Assume P ≥ n.

1. (“If” — printed: trivial.) Suppose d_W(T_j,T) → 0 for every W ⊂⊂ U. Let ω ∈ Dⁿ(U) and choose W ⊂⊂ U open with tsupport ω ⊆ W. Given ε > 0, for large j there are integer multiplicity R, S with T_j − T = ∂R + S and M_W(S) + M_W(R) < ε (definition of the infimum). Then |T_j(ω) − T(ω)| = |R(dω) + S(ω)| ≤ M_W(R)‖dω‖ + M_W(S)‖ω‖ ≤ ε(‖dω‖ + ‖ω‖). Hence T_j ⇀ T.

2. (“Only if” — reduction to subsequences.) Assume T_j ⇀ T. Since M_W ≤ M_{W″} for W ⊆ W″ (`massOn_mono`), d_W ≤ d_{W″}; so it suffices to treat nonempty W (if W = ∅ then M_W ≡ 0 and the decomposition R = 0, S = T_j − T, which is integer multiplicity, gives d_∅(T_j,T) = 0; if U = ∅ all currents vanish). It suffices to show: for every W ⊂⊂ U and every subsequence of (T_j) there is a further subsequence along which d_W(T_j,T) → 0 (a real sequence all of whose subsequences have subsequences tending to 0 tends to 0). Fix W ⊂⊂ U and a subsequence, still denoted T_j.

3. (Integrality of boundaries.) For each j, M_V(∂T_j) ≤ B_V < ∞ for all V ⊂⊂ U, so ∂T_j is integer multiplicity by `BoundaryRectifiability`. Similarly every integer multiplicity current of the class I of 7.1 has integer multiplicity boundary.

4. (Localization — printed (4) with the weak convergence of the localized currents.) Choose an open W′ with closure(W) ⊆ W′ ⊂⊂ U and let φ(x) := dist(x, ℝ^P∖W′) (1-Lipschitz), 2r₀ := min_{closure W} φ > 0, and A_s := {x ∈ U : φ(x) ≥ s} for s ∈ (r₀/2, r₀) (compact ⊆ W′, ⊇ closure W). (i) Measures: the functions F_j(s) := μ_{T_j}({φ ≥ s}) are nonincreasing and bounded by B_{W′}; by Helly's selection theorem a subsequence (not relabelled) converges pointwise on (0, ∞) to a nonincreasing F, which is continuous outside a countable set. (ii) Slices: apply `SlicingTheorem` to each T_j with f = φ, W′, L_W = 1, (a,b) = (r₀/2, r₀): the slices S^j_s satisfy ∫_{r₀/2}^{r₀}g_j ≤ M_{W′}(T_j) ≤ B_{W′} with g_j ≥ M_{W′}(S^j_s); by Fatou, ∫ liminf_j g_j ≤ B_{W′}, so for a.e. s, liminf_j M(S^j_s) < ∞ (spt S^j_s ⊆ {φ = s} ⊆ W′). (iii) Fix s ∈ (r₀/2,r₀) which is a continuity point of F (all but countably many s) and has liminf_j M(S^j_s) < ∞ (a.e. s), and such that every S^j_s is integer multiplicity (a.e. s, T_j integer multiplicity); such s exist (a full-measure set); pass to a subsequence with sup_j M(S^j_s) < ∞. Put T′_j := T_j⌞A_s, T′ := T⌞A_s. Then T′_j, T′ are integer multiplicity (P2), spt ⊆ A_s ⊆ W′, ∂T′_j = (∂T_j)⌞A_s − S^j_s (from `IsSlice`: T_j⌞A_s = T_j − T_j⌞{φ<s}), so sup_j(M(T′_j) + M(∂T′_j)) ≤ B_{W′} + sup_jM(S^j_s) =: M₀ < ∞, and ∂T′_j is integer multiplicity (`BoundaryRectifiability`, or P2 with Step 3 and the integrality of a.e. slice). (iv) T′_j ⇀ T′: for ω ∈ Dⁿ(U) and 0 < η < s − r₀/2, let χ_η be smooth with χ_η = 1 on {φ ≥ s}, χ_η = 0 on {φ ≤ s − η}, 0 ≤ χ_η ≤ 1 (smooth function of a mollified φ). Then |T′_j(ω) − T_j(χ_ηω)| ≤ ‖ω‖μ_{T_j}({s−η < φ < s}) ≤ ‖ω‖(F_j(s−η) − F_j(s)), and likewise |T′(ω) − T(χ_ηω)| ≤ ‖ω‖μ_T({s−η < φ < s}). Since T_j(χ_ηω) → T(χ_ηω), limsup_j|T′_j(ω) − T′(ω)| ≤ ‖ω‖[(F(s−η) − F(s)) + μ_T({s−η<φ<s})] → 0 as η ↓ 0 (continuity of F at s; continuity of the finite measure μ_T⌞W′). (v) Back to T_j: T_j − T = (T′_j − T′) + Z_j with Z_j := T_j⌞(U∖A_s) − T⌞(U∖A_s), integer multiplicity (P2) with M_W(Z_j) = 0 because W ⊆ {φ > s} and Z_j vanishes on forms supported there. Hence if T′_j − T′ = ∂R + S with R, S integer multiplicity then T_j − T = ∂R + (S + Z_j) and d_W(T_j,T) ≤ M_W(S) + M_W(R) (S + Z_j is integer multiplicity, M_W(S + Z_j) ≤ M_W(S)). So it suffices to find a subsequence with d_W(T′_j, T′) → 0, and for this we may assume spt T_j ⊆ A_s, sup_j(M(T_j) + M(∂T_j)) ≤ M₀ and T_j ⇀ T (this is printed (4)). Let W̃ be open with A_s ⊆ … ⊆ closure(W′) ⊆ W̃ ⊂⊂ U and δ := dist(closure W′, ℝ^P ∖ W̃) > 0.

5. (Total boundedness — printed (1)–(3), pigeonhole form.) Extend each T_j to ℝ^P (P3). For ρ > 0 with 2√P ρ < δ, (P5) applied to T_j (with K := closure W′) gives an integer lattice chain Pc_j^{(ρ)} = Σ_{F∈𝓛_n(ρ)}β_F[[F]] and integer multiplicity R_j^{(ρ)}, S_j^{(ρ)} with T_j − Pc_j^{(ρ)} = ∂R_j^{(ρ)} + S_j^{(ρ)}, M(Pc_j^{(ρ)}) ≤ CM₀, M(R_j^{(ρ)}) + M(S_j^{(ρ)}) ≤ CρM₀, and all supports in {dist(·, closure W′) < 2√Pρ} ⊆ W̃. The set of such chains is finite: only the finitely many faces meeting the bounded set {dist(·, closure W′) < 2√Pρ} can carry β_F ≠ 0, and |β_F|ρⁿ ≤ M(Pc) ≤ CM₀ (P4) bounds the integers β_F. Hence among infinitely many indices j, infinitely many share the same chain Pc^{(ρ)}; for two such indices j, j′, T_j − T_{j′} = ∂(R_j^{(ρ)} − R_{j′}^{(ρ)}) + (S_j^{(ρ)} − S_{j′}^{(ρ)}) with integer multiplicity terms (P2), global mass ≤ 2CρM₀ and supports in W̃.

6. (Cauchy subsequence — printed (5).) Choose ρ_r ↓ 0 with 2√Pρ_r < δ and 2Cρ_rM₀ ≤ 2^{−r}. Inductively pick infinite index sets J₁ ⊇ J₂ ⊇ ⋯ such that all j ∈ J_r share the same chain at scale ρ_r (Step 5), and j₁ < j₂ < ⋯ with j_r ∈ J_r. Then for each r, j_r, j_{r+1} ∈ J_r, so (5) T_{j_{r+1}} − T_{j_r} = ∂R_r + S_r with R_r, S_r integer multiplicity, spt R_r ∪ spt S_r ⊆ W̃, M(R_r) + M(S_r) ≤ 2^{−r}.

7. (Limit — printed last paragraph, with 3.13.) The series R^{(ℓ)} := Σ_{r≥ℓ}R_r, S^{(ℓ)} := Σ_{r≥ℓ}S_r converge absolutely in mass, so they define integer multiplicity currents (P2, 3.13) with M(R^{(ℓ)}) + M(S^{(ℓ)}) ≤ 2^{−ℓ+1} and supports in closure(W̃) ⊆ U (restrict them to U, P3). Summing (5) for r = ℓ,…,N−1: T_{j_N} − T_{j_ℓ} = ∂(Σ_{r=ℓ}^{N−1}R_r) + Σ_{r=ℓ}^{N−1}S_r; letting N → ∞ (T_{j_N} ⇀ T; mass convergence of the partial sums implies weak convergence of their boundaries) gives T − T_{j_ℓ} = ∂R^{(ℓ)} + S^{(ℓ)}, i.e. T_{j_ℓ} − T = ∂(−R^{(ℓ)}) + (−S^{(ℓ)}). Hence d_W(T_{j_ℓ},T) ≤ M_W(−S^{(ℓ)}) + M_W(−R^{(ℓ)}) ≤ 2^{−ℓ+1} → 0.

8. (Conclusion.) Steps 4–7 produce, from any subsequence, a further subsequence with d_W(T_j, T) → 0 (via Step 4(v) for the original currents). By Step 2, d_W(T_j,T) → 0 for every W ⊂⊂ U. Together with Step 1 this proves `FlatConvergenceIffWeakConvergence`.
proof_key_steps: 'If': |T_j(ω) − T(ω)| ≤ M_W(R)‖dω‖ + M_W(S)‖ω‖ for a near-optimal decomposition.
'Only if': reduce to showing every subsequence has a further subsequence with d_W → 0; trivial dimensions and W = ∅ handled.
∂T_j integer multiplicity by the sibling boundary rectifiability theorem.

Localize at a good level s of a distance function (slicing + Fatou + Helly): localized currents have bounded mass and boundary mass and converge weakly to the localized limit; the remainder has zero M_W.

Total boundedness via the sibling deformation theorem (or (27)–(37) of 5.1 when P = m+1): finitely many possible lattice chains, pigeonhole gives differences T_j − T_j′ = ∂R + S of small global mass with supports in W̃.
Extract a subsequence with T_{j_{r+1}} − T_{j_r} = ∂R_r + S_r, M(R_r) + M(S_r) ≤ 2^{−r}.

subproblems.title: Rectifiability theorem for currents (Simon 8.1)
subproblems.statement: For all P, m ∈ ℕ, every open U ⊆ ℝ^P and every T ∈ D_{m+1}(U) with M_W(T) + M_W(∂T) < ∞ for all W ⊂⊂ U: if some measure μ with IsMassMeasure T μ has upper density Θ*^{m+1}(μ, x) > 0 for μ-a.e. x, then T = τ(M, θ, ξ) is rectifiable (IsRectifiableCurrent T: M countably (m+1)-rectifiable and Hⁿ-measurable in U, θ > 0 locally integrable, ξ orienting the weighted approximate tangent spaces).
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, 8.1 (Rectifiability Theorem) and its printed proof (pp. 173–175), displays (1)–(13), which use 3.3 and 3.6 of Ch. 1 (density comparison, upper density theorem), Remark 2.37(1),(2) (hence Lemma 2.36 and Remark 2.35 of Ch. 6), the Structure Theorem 3.6 of Ch. 3 (Besicovitch–Federer; Simon gives no proof and refers to [Fed69, 3.3.13] and [Ros84]; see also Mattila, *Geometry of Sets and Measures in Euclidean Spaces*, Thm. 18.1), Lemma 3.2 of Ch. 3, the Radon–Nikodym theorem 3.24 of Ch. 1, the Riesz representation 4.14 of Ch. 1 and the approximate tangent space theory of Ch. 3 §1. Book n = m + 1. The printed proof is copied below in numbered form, with the identification of the measure μ in the Lean hypothesis with μ_T and the verification of `IsRectifiableTriple` (weighted tangent spaces, Ch. 3, 1.7–1.9) filled in. Erratum/notation: Θⁿ in the printed hypothesis is the upper density Θ*ⁿ (as used in (1)–(3) and in the Lean statement); “Structure Theorem 3.8 of Ch. 3” in the preamble of §8 refers to the Rectifiability Theorem for sets, which Simon derives from the Structure Theorem 3.6 and Lemma 3.2 of Ch. 3, and the proof uses 3.6 and 3.2 directly; “1.15 of Ch. 1” (in 2.37) is the inner regularity of Radon measures. Correction of the previous draft: the frozen contract allows every ambient dimension P, including P < m+1 and P = m+1. Step 0 below proves the case P < m+1 directly (all (m+1)-forms on ℝ^P vanish, so T = 0 = τ(∅,1,0) with the empty rectifiable triple) before any dimension-dependent result is invoked, and justifies, for the top-dimensional case P = m+1, each geometric result cited in Steps 1–8 (or replaces it by an elementary argument); no dimension hypothesis is added.

Setting. U ⊆ ℝ^P open, T ∈ D_n(U) (n = m+1) with M_W(T) + M_W(∂T) < ∞ for all W ⊂⊂ U; μ is a measure with `IsMassMeasure T μ` (μ(ℝ^P∖U) = 0 and μ(W) = M_W(T) for every open W ⊂⊂ U) and Θ*ⁿ(μ,x) := `dimensionalUpperDensity μ n univ x` = limsup_{r↓0} μ(B̄_r(x))/(ω_n rⁿ) > 0 for μ-a.e. x. Hⁿ = μHE[n].

Preliminaries.
(P1) Representation (2.7) and identification of μ. By the vector Riesz theorem (Ch. 1, 4.14) applied to the ‖·‖-continuous extension of T to continuous compactly supported forms, T(ω) = ∫⟨ω,T⃗⟩dμ_T with μ_T a Radon measure on the locally compact space U (finite on compact subsets of U), extended by zero to ℝ^P (μ_T(ℝ^P∖U) = 0; μ_T need not be finite on compact subsets of ℝ^P meeting ∂U, and this is never used), |T⃗| = 1 μ_T-a.e. (|·| the Euclidean coefficient norm of n-vectors, w ↦ (Σ_β (w^β)²)^{1/2} with w^β = w(dx^β), dual to `covectorEuclideanNorm`), μ_T(W) = M_W(T) for open W ⊆ U (mollification shows that the suprema over continuous and over smooth forms agree). μ and μ_T agree on the π-system of open sets W ⊂⊂ U, which generates the Borel σ-algebra of U, and U is a countable union of such W with finite measure; hence μ⌞U = μ_T⌞U, and μ(ℝ^P∖U) = 0 = μ_T(ℝ^P∖U), so μ = μ_T. The same applies to ∂T: ∂T(ω) = ∫⟨ω,∂T⃗⟩dμ_{∂T}.
(P2) Remark 2.35, Lemma 2.36, Remark 2.37 (printed). (a) 2.35: a top-dimensional current Y ∈ D_n(V), V ⊆ ℝⁿ open, with M_W(Y), M_W(∂Y) < ∞ is Y(a dx) = ∫aθ dLⁿ with θ ∈ BV_loc(V). (b) 2.36: if E ⊆ U is closed and Lⁿ(p_α(E)) = 0 for every coordinate projection p_α : ℝ^P → ℝⁿ (α ∈ I(n,P)), then T⌞E = 0 whenever M_W(T), M_W(∂T) < ∞ for all W ⊂⊂ U. Printed proof: write ω = Σ_αω_αdx^α, so T(ω) = Σ_α(p_{α#}(T⌞ω_α))(dy) (1), where M(∂(T⌞ω_α)) ≤ M_W(∂T)|ω_α| + M_W(T)|dω_α| < ∞; by (a) p_{α#}(T⌞ω_α) = θ_α[[p_α(U)]] with θ_α ∈ BV, hence p_{α#}(T⌞ω_α)⌞p_α(E) = 0 and (2) M(p_{α#}(T⌞ω_α)) ≤ M_W(T⌞(ℝ^P∖E))|ω_α|; so (3) M_W(T) ≤ CM_W(T⌞(ℝ^P∖E)), i.e. (4) μ_T(W∩E) ≤ Cμ_T(W∖E); taking W_q ↓ K for compact K ⊆ E gives μ_T(K) = 0, and inner regularity gives μ_T(E) = 0. (c) 2.37(1): if C ⊆ U is Borel with Hⁿ(C) = 0 then μ_T(C) = 0 (closed subsets E of C have Lⁿ(p_α(E)) ≤ Hⁿ(E) = 0; inner regularity), i.e. μ_T ≪ Hⁿ. (d) 2.37(2): if Q is an orthogonal transformation of ℝ^P and E ⊆ U with Lⁿ(p_α(Q(E))) = 0 for all α, then μ_T(E) = 0 (apply (b) to Q_#T, whose mass measure is the image of μ_T; inner regularity reduces to closed E).
(P3) Ch. 1, 3.3 (density comparison; SimonGMT `simon_theorem_3_3`, stated there for Simon's Hausdorff outer measure, which is a fixed positive multiple of μH[n] as is μHE[n]; all uses below are qualitative — null sets and finiteness — or absorb the constant): for a Radon measure ν on U, A ⊆ U and t > 0, Hⁿ({x ∈ A : Θ*ⁿ(ν,x) > t}) ≤ t⁻¹ν(A) (outer measures). Simon's 3.3 is stated with the density relative to a set A₂ ⊇ A₁, Θ*ⁿ(ν,A₂,x); to obtain the displayed form for an arbitrary A, use outer regularity: for ε > 0 choose an open V with A ⊆ V ⊆ U and ν(V) ≤ ν(A) + ε, apply 3.3 with A₁ := {x ∈ A : Θ*ⁿ(ν,x) > t} and A₂ := V (for x ∈ V open, Θ*ⁿ(ν,V,x) = Θ*ⁿ(ν,x)), and let ε ↓ 0.

Proof.

0. (Dimension cases. The frozen contract allows every ambient dimension P; no dimension hypothesis is added.)
 (a) Case P < n (= m+1): T = 0 and the empty triple. Every n-covector on ℝ^P is 0: for v₁,…,v_n ∈ ℝ^P with n > P the family is linearly dependent, and an alternating multilinear map vanishes on linearly dependent families (Mathlib `AlternatingMap.map_linearDependent`; `Covector (Eucl P) n` consists of continuous alternating maps). Hence every test form ω ∈ Dⁿ(U) is the zero form, and T(ω) = T(0) = 0 by linearity. Take M := ∅, θ :≡ 1, ξ :≡ 0. Then `IsRectifiableTriple U n ∅ θ ξ` holds: ∅ ⊆ U; ∅ is measurable, in particular `NullMeasurableSet ∅ μHE[n]`; ∅ is countably n-rectifiable (`countablyRectifiable_of_measure_zero`, or M₀ := ∅ in Simon Ch. 3, 1.1); positivity of θ on M is vacuous; for every compact K ⊆ U, θ is integrable on ∅ ∩ K = ∅; and the measure Hⁿ⌞∅ is the zero measure, so ξ is a.e. strongly measurable for it and the orientation clause (an “∀ᵐ x ∂(Hⁿ⌞∅)” statement) holds trivially. Finally tauAction n ∅ θ ξ ω = ∫_∅ θ⟨ω,ξ⟩dHⁿ = 0 = T(ω) for every ω. So T = τ(∅,1,0) is rectifiable, i.e. `IsRectifiableCurrent T`; the hypotheses on T are not needed in this case. (Steps 1–8 below are not used for P < n; they involve n-planes in ℝ^P, which do not exist then.)
 (b) Case P = n (top dimension). Steps 1–8 below apply, with the following justifications of the cited geometric results in this case (Hⁿ = μHE[n] is Lebesgue measure Lⁿ on ℝⁿ):
  • (P2)(b),(c) [Lemma 2.36, Remark 2.37(1)]: for P = n the only multi-index is α = (1,…,n) and p_α = id, so the printed proof of 2.36 reduces to Remark 2.35 (P2)(a): T(a dx¹∧⋯∧dxⁿ) = ∫aθ_T dLⁿ with θ_T ∈ BV_loc(U), whence μ_T = |θ_T|Lⁿ⌞U; in particular μ_T(E) = 0 whenever Lⁿ(E) = 0, i.e. μ_T ≪ Hⁿ. (P2)(d) is not needed.
  • Step 3 [Structure Theorem, Lemma 3.2 of Ch. 3]: not needed. Every subset of ℝⁿ is countably n-rectifiable in the sense of Ch. 3, 1.1 (M ⊆ id(ℝⁿ), and the identity is Lipschitz), so the set M of Step 3 is countably n-rectifiable directly (and, consistently, a purely n-unrectifiable subset of ℝⁿ is Hⁿ-null, so (6) holds trivially).
  • Step 5 [Ch. 3, Theorem 1.9]: replaced by the Lebesgue differentiation theorem. Let θ̄ := θ1_M (θ from Step 4, extended by 0), which is in L¹_loc(U). For Lⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M, x is a Lebesgue point of θ̄ with θ̄(x) = θ(x) > 0. For such x, f ∈ C_c(ℝⁿ) with spt f ⊆ B_R(0) and λ < dist(x, ℝⁿ∖U)/R, we have η_{x,λ}(M) = {z : x+λz ∈ M}, so ∫_{η_{x,λ}M}f(z)θ(x+λz)dHⁿ(z) = ∫_{ℝⁿ}f(z)θ̄(x+λz)dz and |∫f(z)θ̄(x+λz)dz − θ(x)∫_{ℝⁿ}f| ≤ sup|f|·λ^{−n}∫_{B_{λR}(x)}|θ̄(y) − θ̄(x)|dy → 0. Hence `HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt n M θ x ℝⁿ` (finrank ℝⁿ = n), i.e. T_xM = ℝⁿ, for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M. The rest of Step 5 (Lebesgue points of ξ, the blow-up formula (11)) is dimension-free.
  • Step 7 [orientation]: there is no index j ≥ n+1; instead use that Λ_n(ℝⁿ) is one-dimensional. Every n-covector on ℝⁿ equals α(e₁,…,e_n)·dx with dx := dx¹∧⋯∧dxⁿ (an alternating n-form on an n-dimensional space is a multiple of the determinant), so every n-vector w satisfies w(α) = α(e₁,…,e_n)w(dx), i.e. w = w(dx)·simpleNVector(e₁,…,e_n), and |w| = |w(dx)| in the Euclidean coefficient norm of (P1) (the only multi-index is (1,…,n)); the operator norm of `NVector` gives the same value, since ‖dx‖ = 1 by Hadamard's inequality. Since |ξ(x)| = 1, ξ(x) = ±simpleNVector(e₁,…,e_n), and (e₁,…,e_n) is an orthonormal basis of T_xM = ℝⁿ. (Step 6 is then not needed.)
  • Steps 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and the preliminaries (P1), (P3) (Riesz representation, density comparison, Radon–Nikodym, Besicovitch differentiation) are valid in every dimension, in particular for P = n.
 (c) Case P > n. Then ℓ := P − n ≥ 1 and ℝ^P = ℝ^{n+ℓ} is the setting of Simon Ch. 3 (codimension ℓ ≥ 1), so the Structure Theorem 3.6 of Ch. 3, Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 1.9 apply verbatim, and Steps 1–8 are used as written.
 From now on assume P ≥ n.

1. (Printed (1)–(3).) By (P3), for every A ⊆ W, W ⊂⊂ U open, and t > 0: (1) Hⁿ{x ∈ A : Θ*ⁿ(μ_T,x) > t} ≤ t⁻¹μ_T(A) ≤ t⁻¹μ_T(W). Letting t → ∞ and exhausting U: (2) Hⁿ{x ∈ U : Θ*ⁿ(μ_T,x) = ∞} = 0. The same argument with ∂T: (3) Hⁿ{x ∈ U : Θ*ⁿ(μ_{∂T},x) = ∞} = 0.

2. (Printed (4)–(5).) The sets in (2), (3) are Borel (Θ*ⁿ of a Radon measure is Borel, Ch. 1, 3.2) and Hⁿ-null, so by (P2)(c): (4) μ_T{x ∈ U : Θ*ⁿ(μ_T,x) = ∞} = 0 and (5) μ_T{x ∈ U : Θ*ⁿ(μ_{∂T},x) = ∞} = 0.

3. (The carrier and its rectifiability — printed (6), (7).) [The structure-theorem argument of this step is for P > n; for P = n, M below is countably n-rectifiable trivially, Step 0(b).] Let M := {x ∈ U : Θ*ⁿ(μ_T,x) > 0} (Borel), M_j := {x ∈ M : Θ*ⁿ(μ_T,x) > 1/j}. By (1), Hⁿ(M_j ∩ W) ≤ jμ_T(W) < ∞ for W ⊂⊂ U, so M is a countable union of sets of finite Hⁿ-measure. Let P′ ⊆ M be purely n-unrectifiable (Ch. 3, 3.1) and Hⁿ-measurable; P′ is a countable union of sets of finite Hⁿ-measure because M is. By the Structure Theorem (Ch. 3, 3.6; Besicovitch–Federer), Hⁿ(p(P′)) = 0 for γ-almost every orthogonal projection p onto n-planes, γ the invariant measure on the Grassmannian. For each α ∈ I(n,P), the map Q ↦ Q⁻¹(span{e_i : i ∈ α}) carries Haar measure on O(P) to γ, and p_α∘Q is the projection onto Q⁻¹(span{e_i : i ∈ α}) followed by an isometry onto ℝⁿ; hence {Q : Hⁿ(p_α(Q(P′))) > 0} is Haar-null for each α, and so is the union over the finitely many α. Thus there is an orthogonal Q with Hⁿ(p_α(Q(P′))) = 0 for all α. Since Hⁿ⌞M is σ-finite, P′ = B ∪ N with B Borel and N contained in a Borel Hⁿ-null set; μ_T(N) = 0 by (P2)(c), and (P2)(d) applies to B (Lⁿ(p_α(Q(B))) ≤ Hⁿ(p_α(Q(P′))) = 0), so μ_T(P′) = 0, and since Θ*ⁿ(μ_T,·) > 1/j on P′ ∩ M_j, (P3) gives Hⁿ(P′ ∩ M_j) ≤ jμ_T(P′) = 0 for all j: (6) Hⁿ(P′) = 0 for every purely unrectifiable P′ ⊆ M. By Lemma 3.2 of Ch. 3 (SimonGMT `simon_lemma_3_2`: an Hⁿ-σ-finite set is the union of a countably n-rectifiable set and a purely n-unrectifiable set), M is countably n-rectifiable. By hypothesis and (P1), μ_T(U∖M) = μ(U∖M) = 0, so (7) μ_T = μ_T⌞M.

4. (Density — printed (8), (9).) By (P2)(c), μ_T ≪ Hⁿ⌞M, and Hⁿ⌞M is σ-finite (Step 3). By the Radon–Nikodym theorem for σ-finite measures (the abstract form recalled before Ch. 1, 3.24; Hⁿ⌞M need not be Radon), (8) μ_T = θHⁿ⌞M with θ ≥ 0 Hⁿ-measurable (choose a Borel version of the [0,∞]-valued density; it is finite Hⁿ⌞M-a.e. by local integrability, and we take θ := its real value, removing the null set where it is ∞ from M below together with {θ = 0}), locally Hⁿ-integrable on M (∫_{M∩K}θ dHⁿ = μ_T(K) < ∞ for compact K ⊆ U). Removing from M the Hⁿ-measurable set {θ = 0} ∩ M (which is μ_T-null) we may assume θ > 0 on M; M stays countably rectifiable and (7),(8) persist. By (P1), (9) T(ω) = ∫_M θ⟨ω,ξ⟩dHⁿ with ξ := T⃗ (μ_T-measurable, |ξ| = 1 Hⁿ-a.e. on M), i.e. T(ω) = `tauAction n M θ ξ ω` for all ω ∈ Dⁿ(U) (the integrand is integrable: |θ⟨ω,ξ⟩| ≤ θ‖ω‖1_{tsupport ω}).

5. (Weighted approximate tangent spaces — Ch. 3, 1.7–1.9 and printed (10)–(11); for P = n the use of Ch. 3, 1.9 is replaced by the Lebesgue-point argument of Step 0(b).) Since M is countably n-rectifiable and θ is positive and locally integrable on M, by Ch. 3, Theorem 1.9 (with Remark 1.8(1); applied to M ∩ B for balls B ⊂⊂ U, since θ is integrable only on compact subsets of U — tangent spaces at points of B do not change) the weighted approximate tangent space T_xM (`HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt n M θ x (T_xM)`) exists for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M: for f ∈ C_c(ℝ^P), lim_{λ↓0}∫_{η_{x,λ}M}f(z)θ(x+λz)dHⁿ(z) = θ(x)∫_{T_xM}f dHⁿ. Moreover, by Lebesgue's differentiation theorem for the Radon measure μ_T = θHⁿ⌞M (Besicovitch differentiation, cf. Ch. 1 §3), for μ_T-a.e. (equivalently Hⁿ-a.e.) x ∈ M: μ_T(B_{λR}(x))⁻¹∫_{B_{λR}(x)}|ξ − ξ(x)|dμ_T → 0 for every R > 0; combined with Θ*ⁿ(μ_T,x) < ∞ (by (4)), i.e. μ_T(B_{λR}(x)) ≤ C_x(λR)ⁿ for small λ, this gives λ⁻ⁿ∫_{M∩B_{λR}(x)}θ|ξ − ξ(x)|dHⁿ → 0 for every R. (The printed argument (10)–(11) obtains the same via the decomposition M = ⋃M_j, M_j ⊆ N_j ∈ C¹, and Θⁿ(μ_T⌞((N_j∖M_j) ∪ ⋃_{k≠j}M_k), x) = 0 for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M_j.) For such x and ω ∈ Dⁿ(ℝ^P), with η_{x,λ}(y) := (y − x)/λ and λ small enough that η_{x,λ}⁻¹(spt ω) ⊆ U: (η_{x,λ#}T)(ω) = ∫_Mθ(y)⟨ω((y−x)/λ), ξ(y)⟩λ⁻ⁿdHⁿ(y) = ∫_{η_{x,λ}M}θ(x+λz)⟨ω(z), ξ(x+λz)⟩dHⁿ(z), hence (11) lim_{λ↓0}η_{x,λ#}T(ω) = θ(x)∫_{T_xM}⟨ω(z), ξ(x)⟩dHⁿ(z) =: S_x(ω) (13), for all ω, at Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M (independent of ω).

6. (Boundary of the blow-up — printed (12).) For x ∈ M with Θ*ⁿ(μ_{∂T},x) < ∞ (μ_T-a.e., hence Hⁿ-a.e. on M by (5) and μ_T = θHⁿ⌞M with θ > 0), and spt ω ⊆ B_R(0): |∂η_{x,λ#}T(ω)| = |η_{x,λ#}∂T(ω)| ≤ ‖ω‖λ^{1−n}μ_{∂T}(B_{λR}(x)) ≤ ‖ω‖λRⁿω_n·sup_{r≤λR}μ_{∂T}(B_r(x))/(ω_nrⁿ) → 0 as λ ↓ 0. Hence S_x = lim η_{x,λ#}T has ∂S_x = 0.

7. (Orientation — printed after (13); this step is for P > n, the case P = n being Step 0(b).) Fix x as in Steps 5–6 with ξ(x) of unit length. Choose coordinates with L := T_xM = ℝⁿ×{0}. For j ≥ n+1, an (n−1)-tuple i₁ < ⋯ < i_{n−1} and ϕ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^P), let ω := y^jϕ dy^{i₁}∧⋯∧dy^{i_{n−1}}; then dω = ϕ dy^j∧dy^{i₁}∧⋯∧dy^{i_{n−1}} + y^j dϕ∧dy^{i₁}∧⋯, and y^j = 0 on L, so 0 = ∂S_x(ω) = S_x(dω) = θ(x)∫_Lϕ⟨dy^j∧dy^{i₁}∧⋯∧dy^{i_{n−1}}, ξ(x)⟩dHⁿ. Since ϕ is arbitrary and θ(x) > 0, ⟨e_j∧e_{i₁}∧⋯∧e_{i_{n−1}}, ξ(x)⟩ = 0, i.e. every coordinate ξ(x)^β with β ⊄ {1,…,n} vanishes. Hence ξ(x) = ±e₁∧⋯∧e_n (|ξ(x)| = 1) = ±`simpleNVector τ` for the orthonormal basis τ = (e₁,…,e_n) of T_xM.

8. (Conclusion: `IsRectifiableTriple U n M θ ξ`.) M ⊆ U; M is Hⁿ-measurable (the Borel set of Step 3 minus the set {θ = 0} for a Borel version of θ), hence `NullMeasurableSet` for Hⁿ; countably n-rectifiable (Step 3); θ > 0 on M; θ integrable on M ∩ K for compact K ⊆ U (Step 4); ξ is Hⁿ⌞M-a.e. strongly measurable (it is μ_T-measurable and μ_T = θHⁿ⌞M with θ > 0); and for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M there is an orthonormal τ spanning the weighted approximate tangent space with ξ(x) = ±simpleNVector τ (Steps 5–7; for P = n, Step 0(b)). Together with T = τ(M,θ,ξ) (Step 4) this shows `IsRectifiableCurrent T`, proving `RectifiabilityTheorem`.
proof_key_steps: Dimension cases: for P < m+1 all (m+1)-covectors vanish, so T = 0 = τ(∅,1,0) with the empty rectifiable triple; for P = m+1 the structure theorem is unnecessary (every subset of ℝⁿ is rectifiable), 2.36 reduces to 2.35, tangent spaces come from Lebesgue points and Λ_n(ℝⁿ) is one-dimensional; for P > m+1 the Ch. 3 results apply with codimension ℓ = P − m − 1 ≥ 1.
Identify μ with the Riesz mass measure μ_T (agreement on open W ⊂⊂ U).
Density comparison (Ch. 1, 3.3): Hⁿ-null sets where Θ*ⁿ(μ_T) or Θ*ⁿ(μ_∂T) is infinite; μ_T ≪ Hⁿ by 2.36–2.37.
M := {Θ*ⁿ(μ_T) > 0} is Hⁿ-σ-finite; purely unrectifiable subsets are null by the Besicovitch–Federer structure theorem and 2.37(2); Lemma 3.2 of Ch. 3 gives M countably rectifiable.
Radon–Nikodym: μ_T = θHⁿ⌞M with θ > 0 locally integrable; T = τ(M,θ,ξ) with ξ = T⃗.
Weighted tangent spaces exist a.e. (Ch. 3, 1.9); blow-ups η_{x,λ#}T converge to θ(x)[[T_xM]] oriented by ξ(x).
∂ of the blow-up vanishes because Θ*ⁿ(μ_∂T, x) < ∞; testing with y^jϕdy^I shows ξ(x) = ±e(T_xM).
Verify all fields of IsRectifiableTriple.

subproblems.title: Integrality of weak limits of integral currents (Simon 8.2)
subproblems.statement: For all P, m ∈ ℕ and every open U ⊆ ℝ^P: if T_j ∈ D_{m+1}(U) are integral currents (T_j and ∂T_j integer multiplicity) with sup_j (M_W(T_j) + M_W(∂T_j)) < ∞ for every open W ⊂⊂ U and T_j ⇀ T ∈ D_{m+1}(U), then T is integer multiplicity.
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, Theorem 8.2, Remarks 8.3(1),(2) and the printed “Proof of 8.2” (pp. 176–179), displays (1)–(10) and footnote 5; Remark 3.12 (p. 149: the case P = n “is a direct consequence of Remark 2.35 and the Compactness Theorem for BV functions”); and the tools it cites: 2.27, 2.30–2.31 (cones), 2.35, 3.2, 3.10, 4.5, 4.9, 6.1, 8.1, Ch. 1 (3.3, 3.11(3) covering, 4.16 compactness of Radon measures) and Ch. 2 (2.6 BV compactness). Book n = m + 1. The printed proof (induction on n) is copied below in numbered form. Points filled in for the exact Lean statement: (a) the printed localization 8.3(1) is carried out with an explicit choice of radii (slicing, Fatou, Helly) and a patching lemma; (b) the case P = n uses Remark 3.12 and the case P < n is trivial, because the isoperimetric theorem 6.1 is stated (and proved) for codimension ℓ ≥ 1; (c) the a.e. inequality (2) M(∂(T⌞B_r)) ≤ f′(r) (printed “by virtue of 4.9”) is derived from the integrated form of 4.9/4.10 in the sibling slicing theorem; (d) the comparison currents S_j^{(δ)} given by 6.1 are first composed with a smooth radial compression so that their supports lie in B̄_{3r_j}(ξ_j) — the printed cone estimate “(by 2.27, 2.30) |(S_j − T⌞B_j)(ω)| ≤ cM(S_j − T⌞B_j)|dω|” needs this support control (6.1 as stated only asserts compact support); (e) in the integrality step the rescaled masses of T_{j′} are kept bounded by choosing x with Θ*ⁿ(ν,x) < ∞ for a weak limit ν of the mass measures, which justifies the printed “(8) remains valid with T_{j′} instead of T”. Errata: “??(2) of Ch. 1” is the covering property 3.11(3) of Ch. 1 (Besicovitch: every Radon measure on ℝ^P has the Symmetric Vitali Property); in the justification of (3) the printed bound δ⁻¹f^{1/n}(δ) ≤ ω_n^{1/n}ε is wrong — from f(δ) < εω_nδⁿ one gets δ⁻¹f^{1/n}(δ) ≤ (ω_nε)^{1/n} — so (3) reads (d/dr)f^{1/n}(r) ≤ 2(ω_nε)^{1/n}, and (4) becomes M(S_r) ≤ c₂ε^{1/(n−1)}M(T⌞B_r(ξ)) for n ≥ 2 (instead of the printed cε); the threshold ε₀ is chosen accordingly (c₂ε₀^{1/(n−1)} ≤ ½), which is all the covering argument needs; “for Lⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M” in (7) means Hⁿ-a.e.; “σ, ρ” in footnote 5 mean ε.

Sibling results used: `RectifiabilityTheorem` (8.1), `IsoperimetricTheorem` (6.1), `SlicingTheorem` (§4), `LipschitzPushforwardIntegerMultiplicity` (3.9; used for smooth maps, where the push-forward of 3.6 is the classical one 2.23–2.24).

Statement proved, by induction on m: (I_m) for all P, all open U ⊆ ℝ^P, all T_j, T ∈ D_{m+1}(U) with T_j and ∂T_j integer multiplicity, sup_j(M_W(T_j) + M_W(∂T_j)) < ∞ for all W ⊂⊂ U, and T_j ⇀ T: T is integer multiplicity. Write n := m + 1.

Preliminaries.
(P1) Representation, restriction, mass (2.7–2.9, 2.14): currents of locally finite mass are X(ω) = ∫⟨ω,X⃗⟩dμ_X, μ_X(W) = M_W(X) (W open), X⌞A the unique restriction with M_W(X⌞A) = μ_X(W∩A), |X(ω)| ≤ M_W(X)‖ω‖ (tsupport ω ⊆ W); mass is weakly lower semicontinuous; M(X) = 0 ⇒ X = 0.
(P2) Integer multiplicity calculus (3.2): 0, restrictions to Borel sets, integer linear combinations, products [[(0,1)]]×X, images under isometries and dilations, and M-limits (3.13) of integer multiplicity currents are integer multiplicity; an integer multiplicity k-current has locally finite mass and its 0-dimensional (k = 0) version is Σ_{x∈D}c(x)δ_x with D locally finite, c ∈ ℤ∖{0}.
(P3) Smooth push-forwards (2.23–2.24) and cones (2.30–2.31, 3.10). If f is smooth and f|spt X proper, f_#X(ω) = X(ζf^#ω) (ζ ∈ C_c^∞(U) with ζ = 1 near the compact set spt X ∩ spt f^#ω; 2.23), ∂f_# = f_#∂, M_W(f_#X) ≤ sup‖Df‖^kM(X), spt f_#X ⊆ closure f(spt X); if X is integer multiplicity so is f_#X (`LipschitzPushforwardIntegerMultiplicity` gives an integer multiplicity S with `IsLipschitzPushforward X f S`; for smooth f its linear maps agree with Df on T_xM a.e., so S = f_#X. In detail: `IsLipschitzPushforward X f S` provides a representation X = τ(M′,θ′,ξ′) with θ′ > 0 real and integrable on compact subsets of U (not necessarily integer valued or ≥ 1) and linear maps L′ with S(ω) = ∫_{M′}θ′⟨ω(f(x)), L′(x)_#ξ′(x)⟩dHᵏ. At Hᵏ-a.e. x ∈ M′ the orthonormal frame τ with ξ′(x) = ±simpleNVector τ spans a weighted tangent space of (M′,θ′) at x, so the directional-derivative clause gives L′(x)τ_i = Df(x)τ_i and hence L′(x)_#ξ′(x) = Df(x)_#ξ′(x). Moreover Hᵏ(M′ ∖ spt X) = 0, because the mass measure of X is μ_X = θ′Hᵏ⌞M′ (|ξ′| = 1 a.e.), μ_X(U ∖ spt X) = 0 and θ′ > 0 on M′. Therefore, using the representation X(ζf^#ω) = ∫_{M′}θ′⟨ζf^#ω, ξ′⟩dHᵏ (ζf^#ω is a test form) and the duality ⟨(f^#ω)(x), ξ′(x)⟩ = ⟨ω(f(x)), Df(x)_#ξ′(x)⟩ (1.9), f_#X(ω) = X(ζf^#ω) = ∫_{M′}θ′ζ⟨ω(f(x)), Df(x)_#ξ′(x)⟩dHᵏ = ∫_{M′}θ′⟨ω(f(x)), L′(x)_#ξ′(x)⟩dHᵏ = S(ω); ζ may be dropped because at Hᵏ-a.e. x ∈ M′ with (f^#ω)(x) ≠ 0 we have x ∈ spt X ∩ spt f^#ω, where ζ = 1. No integrality or lower bound of θ′ is used). For X ∈ D_k(ℝ^P) with compact support and ξ ∈ ℝ^P, the cone ξ⨯X := h_#([[(0,1)]]×X), h(t,x) := ξ + t(x−ξ) (smooth), satisfies ∂(ξ⨯X) = X − ξ⨯∂X for k ≥ 1, ∂(ξ⨯X) = X − X(1)δ_ξ for k = 0 (homotopy formula 2.25 between the constant map ξ and the identity), M(ξ⨯X) ≤ sup_{x∈spt X}|x−ξ|·M(X) (2.27), spt ξ⨯X ⊆ convex hull of {ξ} ∪ spt X, and ξ⨯X is integer multiplicity if X is (P2 product + this paragraph). If ∂X = 0 (k ≥ 1), or k = 0 and X = ∂Y with Y compactly supported (then X(1) = Y(d1) = 0 after cutting off), then X = ∂(ξ⨯X).
(P4) Domains: a current X ∈ D_k(U) with compact support in U extends to X̃ ∈ D_k(ℝ^P) (X̃(ω) := X(χω), χ ∈ C_c^∞(U), 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 near spt X; independent of χ), with ∂X̃ = (∂X)~, the same masses, X̃ = X on D^k(U), integer multiplicity preserved; conversely Y ∈ D_k(ℝ^P) restricts to Y|_U ∈ D_k(U), and Y = τ(M,θ,ξ) gives Y|_U = τ(M∩U,θ,ξ) integer multiplicity. Patching lemma: let X ∈ D_k(U) and suppose every x ∈ U has an open neighbourhood V_x ⊆ U and an integer multiplicity Y_x ∈ D_k(U) with X(ω) = Y_x(ω) whenever tsupport ω ⊆ V_x. Then X is integer multiplicity. Proof: by Lindelöf choose x_i with U = ⋃_iV_i (V_i := V_{x_i}), Y_i = τ(M_i,θ_i,ξ_i). (i) For all i, i′ the currents Y_i, Y_{i′} agree on test forms supported in V_i ∩ V_{i′}, so the ℝ^{#I(k,P)}-valued (I(k,P) = the strictly increasing k-tuples in {1,…,P}) Radon measures θ_iξ_iHᵏ⌞M_i and θ_{i′}ξ_{i′}Hᵏ⌞M_{i′} coincide on V_i ∩ V_{i′}; taking total variations (|ξ| = 1 a.e.), θ_iHᵏ⌞M_i = θ_{i′}Hᵏ⌞M_{i′} there, so Hᵏ((M_i Δ M_{i′}) ∩ V_i ∩ V_{i′}) = 0 (θ > 0), and θ_i = θ_{i′}, ξ_i = ξ_{i′} Hᵏ-a.e. on M_i ∩ M_{i′} ∩ V_i ∩ V_{i′} (Radon–Nikodym uniqueness with respect to Hᵏ⌞(M_i ∪ M_{i′}), which is σ-finite, indeed locally finite in U, because θ_i, θ_{i′} take values in {1,2,…} and are integrable on compact subsets of U). (ii) Let D_i := V_i ∖ ⋃_{j<i}V_j (disjoint Borel sets covering U), M := ⋃_i(M_i ∩ D_i), and θ := θ_i, ξ := ξ_i on M_i ∩ D_i (so θ(x) = θ_i(x) exactly for x ∈ M ∩ D_i). (iii) X = τ(M,θ,ξ): for a test form ω choose finitely many V_1,…,V_I covering tsupport ω and χ_i ∈ C_c^∞(V_i) with Σχ_i = 1 on tsupport ω; then X(ω) = Σ_iY_i(χ_iω) = Σ_i∫_{M_i}θ_iχ_i⟨ω,ξ_i⟩dHᵏ = Σ_i∫_Mθχ_i⟨ω,ξ⟩dHᵏ = ∫_Mθ⟨ω,ξ⟩dHᵏ, using (i) on each V_i ∩ D_j. (iv) `IsRectifiableTriple U k M θ ξ`: M ⊆ U, Hᵏ-measurable, countably k-rectifiable; θ ∈ {1,2,…}; for compact K ⊆ U, K ⊆ V_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ V_I for some I, so K ∩ D_j = ∅ for j > I and ∫_{M∩K}θ = Σ_{j≤I}∫_{M_j∩D_j∩K}θ_j < ∞; ξ is measurable; by (i), (M,θ) agrees with (M_i,θ_i) on V_i up to Hᵏ-null sets, and the weighted approximate tangent space at x ∈ V_i depends only on M ∩ V_i and θ|V_i modulo Hᵏ-null sets (for small r the blow-up integrals only see x + r·spt f ⊆ V_i, and Hᵏ(η_{x,r}Z) = r^{−k}Hᵏ(Z) = 0 for null Z), so the `orients` property of Y_i transfers to (M,θ,ξ) at Hᵏ-a.e. x ∈ M ∩ D_i (where θ(x) = θ_i(x)).
(P5) The case n = 0 (“trivial” in the printed proof): if X_j ∈ D_0(U) are integer multiplicity with sup_jM_W(X_j) < ∞ (W ⊂⊂ U) and X_j ⇀ X, then X is integer multiplicity. Proof: X_j = Σ_{x∈M_j}c_j(x)δ_x, c_j ∈ ℤ∖{0}, Σ_{x∈M_j∩W}|c_j(x)| = M_W(X_j) ≤ C_W; for fixed W pass to a subsequence along which the ≤ C_W points of M_j ∩ W converge to points x_i ∈ closure W with constant integer coefficients a_i; then X(φ) = Σ_ia_iφ(x_i) for φ ∈ C_c^∞(W), i.e. X = Σ_{y∈W}c(y)δ_y with c(y) := Σ_{x_i=y}a_i ∈ ℤ; these local representations are compatible, so X = τ({c ≠ 0}, |c|, sign c), a locally finite integer combination of Dirac masses, which is integer multiplicity (weighted tangent space {0} at isolated points).
(P6) Restrictions converging weakly. Let X_j ⇀ X in U, W ⊆ U open with sup_jμ_{X_j}(W) < ∞ and μ_X(W) < ∞, φ : U → ℝ Lipschitz, and F_j(s) := μ_{X_j}(W ∩ {φ < s}). By Helly's selection theorem a subsequence has F_j → F pointwise, F nondecreasing. If s is a continuity point of F, then X_j⌞{φ < s}(ω) → X⌞{φ < s}(ω) along this subsequence for every test form ω with tsupport ω ⊆ W. (Proof: let χ_η := κ_η∘φ_ε with φ_ε a mollification of φ near tsupport ω (|φ_ε − φ| < η/4 there) and κ_η smooth, κ_η = 1 on (−∞, s−3η/4], κ_η = 0 on [s−η/4, ∞), so χ_η = 1 where φ ≤ s−η and χ_η = 0 where φ ≥ s on tsupport ω; then |X_j⌞{φ<s}(ω) − X_j(χ_ηω)| ≤ ‖ω‖μ_{X_j}(W ∩ {s−η < φ < s}) ≤ ‖ω‖(F_j(s) − F_j(s−η)) → ‖ω‖(F(s) − F(s−η)), similarly |X⌞{φ<s}(ω) − X(χ_ηω)| ≤ ‖ω‖μ_X(W ∩ {s−η<φ<s}), X_j(χ_ηω) → X(χ_ηω), and both error bounds → 0 as η ↓ 0.) If moreover spt X_j ∩ {φ ≤ s} lies in a fixed compact subset of W for all j, then X_j⌞{φ<s} ⇀ X⌞{φ<s} on all test forms (multiply ω by a cutoff ζ ∈ C_c^∞(W), 0 ≤ ζ ≤ 1, ζ = 1 near that compact set).
(P7) Ch. 1, 3.3: Hⁿ({x ∈ A : Θ*ⁿ(ν,x) > t}) ≤ t⁻¹ν(A) for Radon ν; in particular Hⁿ{Θ*ⁿ(ν,·) = ∞} = 0. Ch. 1, 4.16: a sequence of Radon measures with locally bounded masses has a weakly convergent subsequence. Ch. 1, 3.11(3) + 3.10: for a Radon measure ν on ℝ^P, every fine cover by closed balls of a set A of finite ν-measure has a countable disjoint subfamily covering ν-almost all of A.

Proof of (I_m).

1. (Trivial dimensions.) If P < n all n-covectors vanish, so T = 0 is integer multiplicity.

2. (The case P = n — Remark 3.12.) By 2.35 (printed: mollification as in 2.34 and Ch. 2, 2.7, 2.6), each T_j = θ_j[[U]], i.e. T_j(a dx¹∧⋯∧dxⁿ) = ∫aθ_jdLⁿ, with θ_j ∈ BV_loc(U), ∫_W|θ_j| = M_W(T_j), |Dθ_j|(W) = M_W(∂T_j); θ_j is integer valued since T_j is integer multiplicity (T_j = τ(M_j,θ′_j,±e₁∧⋯∧e_n)). By the BV compactness theorem (Ch. 2, 2.6) a subsequence θ_j → θ in L¹_loc(U), and a further subsequence converges a.e., so θ is integer valued. Then T(a dx) = lim T_j(a dx) = ∫aθ dLⁿ, so T = τ({θ ≠ 0}, |θ|, sign(θ)e₁∧⋯∧e_n), which is integer multiplicity (at Lⁿ-a.e. point of {θ ≠ 0} the weighted tangent space of ({θ≠0}, |θ|) is ℝⁿ by Lebesgue's differentiation theorem; e₁∧⋯∧e_n = simpleNVector of the standard frame). Assume from now on P ≥ n + 1.

3. (Inductive hypothesis.) (IH) If n − 1 ≥ 1, (I_{m−1}) holds (degree n − 1, all P, all U); if n − 1 = 0, (P5) holds. In both cases: weak limits of integer multiplicity (n−1)-currents with integer multiplicity boundaries and locally bounded masses and boundary masses are integer multiplicity.

4. (Localization — Remark 8.3(1).) Fix ξ₀ ∈ U and r₀ > 0 with B̄_{2r₀}(ξ₀) ⊆ U, d₀ := |· − ξ₀|, W₀ := B_{2r₀}(ξ₀), Λ₀ := sup_j(M_{W₀}(T_j) + M_{W₀}(∂T_j)). By `SlicingTheorem` (T_j has locally finite mass and boundary mass) the slices S^j_r of T_j by d₀ satisfy ∂(T_j⌞B_r(ξ₀)) = S^j_r + (∂T_j)⌞B_r(ξ₀), are integer multiplicity for a.e. r, and ∫_{r₀/2}^{r₀}M_{W₀}(S^j_r)dr ≤ ∫g_j ≤ M_{W₀}(T_j) ≤ Λ₀ (measurable majorants g_j). By Fatou, liminf_jM(S^j_r) < ∞ for a.e. r ∈ (r₀/2,r₀) (spt S^j_r ⊆ ∂B_r(ξ₀) ⊆ W₀). By (P6) (with φ = d₀, W = W₀) pass to a subsequence with F_j → F (spt(T_j⌞B_r(ξ₀)) ⊆ B̄_r(ξ₀), a fixed compact subset of W₀, so (P6) gives weak convergence on all test forms). Choose r ∈ (r₀/2,r₀) such that all S^j_r are integer multiplicity, liminf_jM(S^j_r) < ∞, and r is a continuity point of F; pass to a further subsequence with sup_jM(S^j_r) < ∞. Then X_j := T_j⌞B_r(ξ₀) and ∂X_j = S^j_r + (∂T_j)⌞B_r(ξ₀) are integer multiplicity (P2), spt X_j ⊆ B̄_r(ξ₀) =: K₀, sup_j(M(X_j) + M(∂X_j)) < ∞, and X_j ⇀ X := T⌞B_r(ξ₀) (P6). Extend to ℝ^P (P4). If we show (Steps 5–12, the special case U = ℝ^P, spt T_j ⊆ K compact) that X̃ is integer multiplicity, then X = X̃|_U is integer multiplicity and T agrees with X on the open ball B_r(ξ₀) ∋ ξ₀; by the patching lemma (P4), T is integer multiplicity. So assume U = ℝ^P, spt T_j ⊆ K (compact), Λ := sup_j(M(T_j) + M(∂T_j)) < ∞, T_j ⇀ T; then spt T ⊆ K.
